Tens of thousands of users are reporting issues with Microsoft products in Canada and the U.S., according to outage tracker Downdetector.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

There were nearly 140,000 reports of problems using Microsoft Outlook as of 1:30 p.m. ET, the website reported.

Microsoft’s service incidents social media account said it was investigating.

“We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” it wrote online.

Issues were also reported with Copilot and Microsoft 365, the subscription suite that includes various apps like Word, Excel, Teams, OneDrive and others.

‘Take your time’

Some Microsoft users took to social media to lament the outage, while others encouraged the company not to fix the issue too quickly.

“Take your time. The peace and quiet is nice LOL,” wrote one user.

“Please leave Outlook down till Friday 5 pm :),” wrote another.

Other outages

Downdetector.com also noted reported issues with Amazon Wed Services (1,350) and Gmail (1,000), shortly after 2 p.m.

This is a breaking news story. More details to come…

items._ogDesc: Shares of Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the global artificial intelligence boom, tumbled Thursday with the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of an affair with a woman reported to be a suspected Chinese spy.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Shares of Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the global artificial intelligence boom, tumbled Thursday with the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of an affair with a woman reported to be a suspected Chinese spy.

The company’s stock has been under pressure for weeks, both because of reporting about the affair and questions about a potential bubble in the AI sector.

Shares fell five per cent in afternoon trading, more than 30 per cent below the company’s all-time high reached just over a month ago.

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to step down in big blow to AI boom

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

“The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia,” wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.

Nvidia is now valued at more than US$4 trillion and has been a major driver in the technology sector. It is one of the reasons the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite index raced higher for most of this year and also part of the reason the index has slumped seven per cent in the past month.

  • Latest updates on company news here

As the crisis unfolded at Nvidia, shares of rivals like AMD, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom have moved sharply higher.

CoreWeave, however slid more than seven per cent. Nvidia owns a stake of approximately 13 per cent in the a data centre and cloud company.

items.title: Roshel, Stellantis met with PMO, Joly’s office in lead up to Brampton assembly plant deal
items.description: Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s most senior staff and a top aide in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Office met with armoured vehicle maker Roshel in advance of its announced purchase of the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Lobby records show both Stellantis and Roshel held high-level meetings with government officials in recent months, including with senior staff in Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s office. (Image credit: The Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s most senior staff and a top aide in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Office met with armoured vehicle maker Roshel in advance of its announced purchase of the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant.
items.body:
OTTAWA/DUBLIN – Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s most senior staff and a top aide in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Office met with armoured vehicle maker Roshel in advance of its announced purchase of the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant.

According to filings in the federal lobbying registry, four top aides in Joly’s office met with Roshel in September and August. The records show both meetings included her then chief of staff Paul Moen and her director of policy David McFarlane. The same two aides met with Roshel again on Oct. 15.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Joly’s office told The Canadian Press on Wednesday that the minister had not met with Roshel prior to the Monday announcement that it would purchase the Stellantis plant. Her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether her team’s meetings with Roshel were sanctioned or if she was briefed on them.

The registry also shows the prime minister’s senior global affairs adviser, Matthew Hall, met with Roshel on Oct. 15. Two sources said the company’s CEO Roman Shimanov attended that meeting.

CTV News is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. The Prime Minister’s Office did not provide a comment to CTV News.

The lobbyist registry also shows the federal government held 10 high-level meetings with Stellantis in September alone. Carney’s deputy chief of staff Tim Krupa joined the final meeting listed on Sept. 29 along with Joly, Moen, and McFarlane.

The registry for Stellantis is up to date only until September and does not include any meetings that may have been held in October. Meetings that were requested by the government are not listed in the registry.

Carney acknowledges awareness of deal

Carney expressed outrage at the sale once it was announced, with the prime minister calling it a “betrayal” of the workers and Canada. But sources told CTV News that the federal government was actively engaged in discussions with both companies about the details of the deal, and privately the government did not stand in the way of it.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday in Dublin, Carney acknowledged that his government was aware of some of the plan and described the plant’s sale to Roshel as a “partial solution.”

“The issue for Stellantis is providing a global solution for the plant,” he said. “So the Roshel deal is a partial solution for the 1000s of workers there.”

“Being informed or being aware of some aspects is not the same as Stellantis providing a global solution for those workers at the plant, which is their obligation,” Carney added.

A senior government official told CTV News on Thursday that Ottawa privately set expectations more broadly relating to Stellantis’s obligations to workers, and those expectations have not been met.

What’s included in the deal?

Full details of the sale agreement and the companies’ plans for the plant have not yet been disclosed. But CTV News has confirmed key elements of the plan that two sources said were shared with the federal government last week.

Included in the proposal is a pledge from Stellantis to pay the pensions for all eligible workers. The plant has been idle since 2023, with more than 2,200 workers on lay-off pay.

In a statement to CTV News Thursday, Stellantis spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin confirmed this element of the plan and said about 60 per cent of the Brampton workforce is retirement eligible.

“It is our priority to engage with Unifor through the collective bargaining process on a fair outcome to support employees,” she said.

Gosselin also confirmed previous reporting from CTV News that Stellantis has offered to pay back $24 million to the government, which was paid out as part of an agreement to retool the plant and keep minimum employment levels.

Records show the government has paid Stellantis at least $222 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor, Ont., plants. The government has not provided a comment to CTV News to address whether Ottawa is in agreement with Stellantis on the sum to be repaid.

Roshel’s CEO has indicated in public comments that a European car company has expressed interest in the plant, should the Roshel purchase go through.

Two sources tell CTV News that executives from Jaguar visited the Stellantis facility on Oct. 14. Shimanov said 25 per cent of the plant would be re-leased by Stellantis, and the rest could be used by a combination of other carmakers and his own company’s defence manufacturing.

In a statement sent to CTV News about the details of the plan that were shared with the government last week, Joly’s spokesperson Mathis Denis said the government “has not been involved in or supportive of the private agreement announced between Stellantis and Roshel.”

“To date, the government’s communications with Stellantis have focused on finding a path forward that protects jobs and maintains manufacturing at the Brampton Assembly Plant,” he said. “Within these discussions, we heard many proposals, none of which reflect our expectations for an acceptable outcome.”

He added that Joly “at no point” endorsed Roshel’s proposal to buy the Stellantis plant.

Denis said the minister and officials are in regular contact with Stellantis as it seeks to resolve the dispute over the payments the government has given the company to keep its operations in Canada. The deal dates back to 2022 and in it Ottawa said it would give the company up to $529 million for Stellantis to retool both its plants in Brampton and Windsor.

“The message from the Minister has been the same from the beginning: uphold your commitments to the workers, the union, and continue your operations. The same expectations of Stellantis have been emphasized directly to Roshel,” Denis said.

Joly will meet with Unifor, Stellantis and representatives with the Ontario government in Toronto on Thursday.

With files from CTV News Ottawa bureau manager Stephanie Ha

items.title: ‘I feel sorry for him’: Minister responds to Poilievre’s comments on immigration plan
items.description: The federal minister of immigration had a response to some sharp comments from the leader of the Conservative Party during a visit to Dieppe, N.B., on Thursday.

items._ogDesc: The federal minister of immigration had a response to some sharp comments from the leader of the Conservative Party during a visit to Dieppe, N.B., on Thursday.
items.body:
The federal minister of immigration had a response to some sharp comments from the leader of the Conservative Party during a visit to Dieppe, N.B., on Thursday.

Lena Metlege Diab, minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, provided more details on a targeted, time-limited measure announced in this year’s budget that will help provinces and territories meet their labour market needs for immigrants who are already living and working in Canada.

The initiative will support the transition to permanent residence of up to 100,000 workers as well as family members in 2027.

  • Download the CTV News App for breaking news alerts and video on all the top stories

“These are people whose skills and experience are already supporting Canadian employers and communities,” said Diab. “These are not people that are arriving new. In some cases, these people have been here for years.”

Diab said the workers have been supporting the economy in key industries in towns and cities across Canada.

“It is the right thing to do,” said Diab. “These are people already living in Canada. They will not put additional pressure on housing, infrastructure and public services. This is a targeted, one-year measure. It is not a new program. It is not a permanent increase to our immigration levels.”

Released last week, the levels plan includes targets for 380,000 permanent residents and 370,000 new temporary residents each year through 2029.

It also comes with a pledge to make upwards of 200,000 longtime temporary residents permanent by the end of next year.

During a press conference in Stellarton, N.S., earlier this week, Diab said half of the 200,000 target will be made up of workers already in Canada and will be chosen in collaboration with the provinces and territories.

The plan has caught the attention of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre who called the federal government’s new immigration measure “bonkers” during a video released Sunday.

“This is insane. Population growth already outstripped housing, health care and jobs for a decade,” said Poilievre in his video.

“I feel sorry for him and the people that are working with him. I really don’t believe he understands Canada,” said Diab on Thursday. “I really feel he doesn’t understand our workers. He doesn’t understand our businesses. He doesn’t understand Canadians, no matter who they are.”

In his video, Poilievre claimed the plan will bring roughly 200,000 more permanent residents each year than when Justin Trudeau was prime minister.

“The arrivals are not the same as admissions,” said Diab. “That 100,000, these are people that are already in the country. These are not coming new. They’re not going to take away things.

“In fact, they are helping you, you and you. In your schools and hospitals and building your homes. That’s what they’re doing. We have these people in our country. They’re working, paying taxes.”

Diab said she understands how some Canadians are rightly concerned.

“We brought in too many people in the past. That is exactly whey we have stabilized our numbers in the last couple of years,” said Diab.

Provinces and territories will be offered program allocations and will be able to decide how much of the additional space they use to transition workers who have established themselves in their communities while meeting their labour market needs.

The Provincial Nominee Program allocations are intended to be used by the end of March to support the transition of workers and family members to permanent residency in 2027.

The governments of each province and territory will be able to identify workers who have already applied for permanent residence and are waiting for a decision.

With files from The Canadian Press

items.title: Canada-U.S. travel turnoff reversing after U.S. midterm elections
items.description: Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States.

items._ogDesc: Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States.
items.body:
MONTREAL — Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up.

Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada.

However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September.

At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

“It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency.

Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies.

“We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said.

“One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.”

Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations.

Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism.

“Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc.

“There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the mindset of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.”

Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips.

“We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.ca.

Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

“I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’”

The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether.

“We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said.

“To market the U.S. is like dynamite.”

Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Top Picks from Stan Wong, Portfolio Manager, Scotia Wealth Management
items.body:
Stan Wong, Portfolio Manager, Scotia Wealth Management

Focus: North American Large Caps & ETFs

Top Picks: Alphabet, iShares Semiconductor ETF, Vanguard Industrials ETF

The outlook for global equities remains constructive despite recent market volatility. The U.S. economy has maintained steady growth, and corporate earnings continue to grow. Persistent inflation and elevated bond yields remain risks, especially for stocks whose valuations leave little room for earnings disappointments.

Technology has seen some of the sharpest swings. In the recent market decline, the Nasdaq-100 fell about 15 per cent from peak to trough, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 40 per cent. The selling pressure extended to companies supplying power and equipment for data centers as investors reassessed the regulatory outlook following the U.S. midterm elections. The selloff may also have been intensified by hedge funds exiting crowded and, in some cases, leveraged positions tied to artificial intelligence.

The market reaction appears to have overstated the long-term risk to AI investment. Permitting delays and power constraints remain legitimate near-term challenges, as they can raise costs and postpone projects. However, global demand for computing capacity continues to grow, several states within the U.S. are competing to attract data center projects, and strategic competition with China gives the U.S. another reason to keep building. For investors, the question is whether share prices have fallen further than the earnings outlook warrants. Order backlogs, margins and cash flow can help gauge whether project delays are starting to weigh on earnings prospects.

At The Stan Wong Group, we continue to favour high-quality large-cap businesses with resilient cash flows, durable competitive advantages and strong growth prospects. We remain disciplined about what we pay for that growth. As always, investment decisions should be made within the context of each investor’s broader total wealth plan.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google
  • Market-moving news, fast: Get the BNN Bloomberg App now
  • Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters

Alphabet (GOOGL NASD)

Alphabet’s recent drawdown of more than 30 per cent has created an unusual opportunity to invest in one of the world’s highest-quality technology companies at a notably lower valuation. The shares now trade at approximately 18 times forward earnings, below their 10-year average of about 20.7 times.

Alphabet is much more than a search company. Its businesses span Search, YouTube, Google Cloud, subscriptions and Waymo, giving it several powerful ways to monetize artificial intelligence. The latest results showed that AI is strengthening rather than disrupting the core business. Revenue increased 25 per cent to US$127.6 billion, while Search revenue grew 12 per cent and query growth reached its fastest pace in five years. Gemini has reached one billion users, demonstrating enormous scale in generative AI.

Google Cloud is becoming a much larger earnings engine. Revenue more than doubled to US$30.7 billion, while operating income more than tripled to US$11.1 billion. Cloud backlog reached US$561 billion, with more than half expected to become revenue within two years, providing strong visibility into future growth.

Meeting that demand requires substantial investment. Alphabet expects 2026 capital expenditures of US$195 billion to US$205 billion, primarily for AI and cloud infrastructure. This is pressuring near-term free cash flow, but approximately US$265 billion in cash and marketable securities gives Alphabet considerable capacity to fund the buildout.

When the shares last crossed the 30 per cent drawdown threshold in September 2022, they gained 36.8 per cent over the following 12 months. Technically, the shares appear to be stabilizing, and a recovery toward the 200-day moving average would confirm improving momentum.

iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX NASD)

The iShares Semiconductor ETF provides diversified exposure to 30 leading semiconductor companies and seeks to track the investment results of the NYSE Semiconductor Index. Major holdings include AMD, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and Intel. Its management fee is 0.33 per cent.

Semiconductors are the essential building blocks of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, smartphones, automobiles, industrial automation and defence. AI-driven demand is broadening beyond graphics processors into memory, networking chips, power-management semiconductors and advanced packaging. Global AI-server revenue is projected to increase 64 per cent in 2026 to US$462 billion, with AI servers expected to represent 77 per cent of total server revenue. SOXX provides exposure across this expanding value chain without requiring investors to identify one eventual winner.

The recent selloff has dramatically improved valuations. The NYSE Semiconductor Index currently trades at approximately 15 times forward earnings, nearly half the peak multiple reached during 2025 and back to levels last seen in 2022.

SOXX recently experienced a drawdown of 40 per cent. Bloomberg analysis of previous SOXX drawdowns of at least 40 per cent over the past 25 years shows an average 12-month forward return of 25.3 per cent, with positive returns 75 per cent of the time. While history does not guarantee the same result, severe semiconductor corrections have often created attractive long-term buying opportunities.

From a technical perspective, the correction has reset momentum and created a more attractive entry point. SOXX has begun to stabilize and is working back toward its 200-day moving average. A recovery above that level would provide further confirmation of improving momentum. Compelling valuations and a powerful growth outlook reinforce the long-term opportunity.

Vanguard Industrials ETF (VIS NYSE)

The Vanguard Industrials ETF provides exposure to nearly 400 U.S. industrial companies for a low expense ratio of 0.09 per cent. Major holdings include Caterpillar, GE Aerospace, RTX, Eaton and Deere. This diversified portfolio captures several important long-term investment themes.

The U.S. industrial cycle is gaining momentum. Core capital-goods orders increased 14.1 per cent year over year, signalling stronger business investment. Manufacturing reshoring, infrastructure renewal, aerospace and defence spending, electrification and grid modernization are creating sustained demand for machinery, transportation, engineering and electrical equipment.

Artificial intelligence provides another powerful growth engine. Data center construction spending is forecast to increase 33 per cent in 2026 and a further 25 per cent in 2027. The benefits extend beyond technology companies because these facilities require electrical equipment, cooling systems, automation, construction machinery and reliable power. Many VIS holdings provide the physical infrastructure required to build and operate the AI economy.

The ETF combines established industrial leaders with companies positioned at the core of the power and data center buildout, reducing reliance on any one company or theme. It also provides exposure to a recovery in traditional capital spending beyond AI.

From a technical perspective, VIS recently experienced a drawdown of almost 15 per cent following a strong multi-year advance. The pullback has improved the risk-reward profile, and the ETF is now recovering toward its 200-day moving average. A sustained move above that level would strengthen the technical outlook. Improving capital spending, durable secular growth drivers and broad diversification reinforce our positive view.

items.title: Champagne says energy investments set the stage for Canada's future economic growth
items.description: Canada’s finance minister says Ottawa is investing in energy infrastructure to create a foundational base for the new technologies that will power the 21st century economy.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s finance minister says Ottawa is investing in energy infrastructure to create a foundational base for the new technologies that will power the 21st century economy.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Canada’s finance minister says Ottawa is investing in energy infrastructure to create a foundational base for the new technologies that will power the 21st century economy.

François-Philippe Champagne told a group of business people in Halifax this morning that history has shown economies with plenty of energy resources do better in the long run.

He said the world is moving toward electrification in almost every area of the economy, including the transport, manufacturing and industrial sectors.

Canada has seen an explosion in interest from artificial intelligence companies in recent months as they look to spend billions building energy-hungry data centres that can take advantage of the country’s abundant resources.

However, AI stocks have been falling in recent weeks and the value of AI chip behemoth Nvidia plummeted today amid the resignation of its CEO over a deepening sex and spying scandal.

Champagne said stock markets are always going to fluctuate, but if Canada invests in a strong energy foundation, the demand and economic benefits will follow.

“When you invest in foundational pieces like energy, you cannot be wrong because energy will be key to power our economy for now and obviously the future,” Champagne told reporters following the event.

items.title: Canadian Tire courts gift shoppers with price cuts as costs squeeze consumers
items.description: Canadian Tire has dropped the prices on more than 5,000 goods, including gift wrap and ornaments, and expanded its toy department and Hudson’s Bay products.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Shoppers come and go from a Canadian Tire store in Ottawa on Friday, Aug. 11, 2023. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Sean Kilpatrick</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canadian Tire has dropped the prices on more than 5,000 goods, including gift wrap and ornaments, and expanded its toy department and Hudson’s Bay products.
items.body:
Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. executives are working to morph the business into more of a gifting destination, even as shoppers continue to face economic challenges.

The retailer, which is also behind SportChek, Mark’s and Party City, has dropped the prices on more than 5,000 goods, including gift wrap and ornaments, and expanded its toy department and offerings using the Hudson’s Bay stripes.

The goal is to capture a holiday market that chief executive Greg Hicks estimates is worth more than $5 billion and then build on it throughout the year.

  • Latest updates on company news here

“That means not just leaning into having the right products to gift but also (looking at) how we get consumers to have us more front of mind when they’re looking for gifts for other occasions, like birthdays or Mother’s Day,” Hicks said Thursday on a call with analysts to discuss the company’s latest results.

Canadian Tire’s push to provide more gifting inspiration comes as consumers are heading into the holiday season facing an economic avalanche. 

Tariff tensions and the war in Iran have driven up household expenses like gas, causing a big drop in consumer confidence and creating “a negative shock that’s shrinking the economy’s potential,” Hicks said.

While shoppers are proving to be more resilient than some expected, he’s noticed many Canadians are taking a more cautious approach to spending but will still spend when the value proposition feels right to them.

“The bar is higher,” Hicks explained. “They want value, they want relevance, they want convenience, they want price and they want to shop at a place that they trust.”

Canadian Tire is forecasting that those demands will last for anywhere from another year to 18 months.

Already, the conditions are colliding with a warm autumn, weighing on sales, which tend to grow as the temperature drops.

“We’re off to a slower start in October. Clearly, winter has not showed up,” chief financial officer Darren Myers said on the same call as Hicks, comparing the recent weather to last year, when parts of the country were stormy. “There’s a lot of the quarter left to play but we do need the weather to turn.”

The insights came after Canadian Tire increased its dividend and reported its third-quarter profit rose compared with a year ago.

The Toronto-based retailer will now pay a quarterly dividend of $1.825 per share, up from $1.80 per share.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The increased payment to shareholders dovetailed with Canadian Tire revealing it earned net income attributable to shareholders of $219.6 million or $4.27 per diluted share for its latest quarter, up from $169.1 million or $3.13 per diluted share a year earlier.

On a normalized basis, it earned $4.27 per diluted share during the quarter ended Oct. 3, up from a normalized profit of $3.78 per diluted share a year ago.

Revenue totalled $4.32 billion, up from $4.11 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

Overall comparable sales rose 3.2 per cent across the company’s banners. Canadian Tire comparable sales increased 3.2 per cent, while SportChek also saw a gain of 3.2 per cent. Mark’s reported 3.3 per cent in comparable sales growth.

The results pushed Canadian Tire’s share price up by almost seven per cent or $14 to about $218 in mid-morning trading.  

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items.description: The FCT president adds the chief executive role, taking the helm at Canada’s title insurance provider
items.content: <p>The FCT president adds the chief executive role, taking the helm at Canada’s title insurance provider</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639301069149411183.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The FCT president adds the chief executive role, taking the helm at Canada’s title insurance provider
items.body:
FCT, Canada’s provider of title insurance and real estate technology, has named Daniela DeTommaso as president and chief executive officer, effective January 1, 2027.

DeTommaso, who has led the Oakville, Ontario-based company as president since June 2021, will assume the dual role. 

Michael LeBlanc, FCT’s current chief executive, shifts his focus to president of the international division at parent company First American Financial Corporation, based in Santa Ana, California.

The appointment marks more than 30 years at FCT for DeTommaso, who began her career in the company’s legal department before rising through increasingly senior roles across the organization.

From legal counsel to chief executive

DeTommaso’s trajectory reflects an unusually deep institutional knowledge. By the late 2000s, she was leading FCT’s residential lending solutions group, overseeing its mortgage-facing product lines.

She later guided FCT’s data and innovation strategy before being elevated to president in 2021 to oversee all product, operations, sales, and marketing functions. She holds an LL.B. and serves as vice-chair of Hospice Vaughan in Ontario.

Earlier this year, she joined the judging panel for CMP’s 2026 Top 50 Women of Influence, a recognition in which FCT has long been an active participant. 

“Daniela is an exceptional leader whose strategic vision, sound judgment and commitment to our customers and people have made a lasting impact on FCT,” LeBlanc said.

“Having worked alongside Daniela for nearly three decades, I have seen firsthand her ability to bring people together, navigate change and translate strategy into meaningful results. I have tremendous confidence in her ability to lead FCT forward.”

DeTommaso acknowledged both the responsibility and the continuity ahead.

“FCT’s strength comes from our people, customer-focused culture and commitment to continually evolve,” she said.

“I look forward to working with our talented teams to build on that foundation, further strengthen our business and deliver solutions that create lasting value for our customers and partners.”

An appointment that matters beyond FCT

Her elevation to chief executive carries significance across the broader Canadian mortgage sector. According to CMP’s 2026 roundtable of Canadian mortgage finance leaders, women hold just 4% of CEO roles in the Canadian mortgage industry. 

As chief executive, DeTommaso will bear responsibility for strategy, people, customer relationships, operational discipline, and capital allocation.

LeBlanc will continue to oversee FCT as part of his international remit, to whom DeTommaso will report.

Founded in 1991 and headquartered in Oakville, Ontario, FCT is a wholly owned subsidiary of First American Financial Corporation.

The company employs more than 1,200 professionals across Canada and serves approximately 450 lenders, 43,000 legal professionals, and 5,000 recovery experts, as well as mortgage brokers, real estate agents, and builders nationwide.

Its product suite covers residential and commercial title insurance, property intelligence, default solutions, and digital real estate transaction technology across the full property lifecycle.

items._ogDesc: Greater Toronto’s purpose-built rental vacancy hits 13.3% as completions reach a record, with another 34,545 units under construction.
items.body:
The Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) rental market is tightening—if you exclude new supply. A new report from Urbanation shows a falling vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rental buildings in Q3. However, including new buildings still trying to find their first tenants reveals roughly 1 in 8 units are vacant, with a lot more in the pipeline.

Greater Toronto Rental Vacancy Reaches 13.3% Including New Buildings

When we reported on Q1 back in May, nearly 1 in 19 apartments sat vacant in Greater Toronto’s stabilized rental buildings completed since 2000. That’s now dropped to 1 in 33, with the vacancy rate falling from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch here is the term stabilized, which Urbanation defines as having reached 95% occupancy.

Stabilized is an industry term used to assess buildings that have moved beyond their initial leasing phase and established an operating income. However, focusing on those buildings excludes newer projects still struggling to attract tenants—even though those vacant apartments compete for the same renters.

A more comprehensive look tells a very different story. The rental vacancy rate jumps to 13.3% in Q3 when including buildings in the “lease up” phase to hit that 95% goal, up from 12.1% last year. The 1 in 33 vacant units looks more like over 1 in 8 when those are included.

New Rental Apartments Arrive Faster Than Tenants Fill Them

The number of occupied purpose-built rental apartments rose by 1,911 units in Q3. Builders completed a record 2,704 apartments over the same three months, exceeding the growth in occupied units by 793. Even during the busiest leasing quarter of the year, new supply outpaced demand.

That gap comes despite record growth in occupied apartments. Through September, the number rose by 5,092 units, up 22% from the same period last year.

Rents after incentives remained 1.5% below a year earlier in purpose-built rental buildings surveyed in both periods. Landlords also pulled back on incentives: 60% of projects offered them, down from 67% in Q2, while one month of free rent replaced two months as the most common offer. Headline incentives shrank, but rents remain lower than last year even after accounting for fewer incentives.

Greater Toronto Has 34,500 Purpose-Built Rentals Under Construction

Even as the overall purpose-built vacancy rises, a lot more supply is on the way. Builders started 12,106 purpose-built rental units through September, up 82% from the same period last year and already exceeding the full-year total for 2025. That brought the number of units under construction to 34,545. Purpose-built rentals now account for nearly half of all apartments under construction in the GTHA.

Urbanation expects the drop in condo completions to outweigh the rise in purpose-built rental units. The shift isn’t an accident, as it follows policymakers’ push to use taxpayer-backed incentives to grow institutional investment in the sector.

items.title: Canadian building permits slide as multi-unit plans retreat
items.description: Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally
items.content: <p>Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639300980349360319.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally
items.body:
The total value of building permits issued across Canada fell 4.1% to $12.9 billion in September, Statistics Canada reported Thursday. A sharp pullback in multi-family residential intentions signalled continued strain on new housing supply.

On a constant dollar basis (2023=100), permit values declined 4.5% from August but remained 1.9% above the same month a year earlier.

Building permits, surveyed across approximately 2,400 municipalities representing 95% of the country’s population, are a leading indicator of construction activity, though issuance does not guarantee that construction will proceed.

Multi-family weakness dominates the residential slide

Residential building permit values fell 5.8% to $7.8 billion in September. The multi-family component drove the decline, sliding $529.3 million to $5.1 billion.

British Columbia (-$292.1 million) and Alberta (-$186.8 million) recorded the steepest retreats, with eight provinces and one territory contributing to the drop.

Year-to-date, residential permit values have fallen 5.2% in 2026, according to Statistics Canada.

Single-family permits moved in the opposite direction, rising $53.6 million to $2.7 billion, largely on strength from Ontario (+$103.3 million).

Non-residential intentions edged down $77.1 million to $5.1 billion, as a decline in institutional construction (-$171.5 million) was partially offset by industrial permit growth (+$90.9 million), driven by Ontario and Nova Scotia.

What September’s data signals for the construction pipeline

The September result caps a weak third quarter. Total building permit values fell $1.5 billion to $38.8 billion in Q3, a 3.6% quarterly drop, with non-residential permits recording their sharpest quarterly decline since Q2 2020.

Nationally, 71,300 homes were authorized for construction in Q3, down from 78,500 in the same period of 2025. That's a year-over-year decline of roughly 9.2%.

For mortgage brokers navigating this constrained supply environment, managing client expectations around future inventory has become central to daily practice.

Major banks and homebuilders are pressing Ottawa to act, having urged the federal government to ease mortgage qualification rules for first-time buyers of newly built homes in a 29-point reform plan released this week.

“Building permits provide an early signal of future residential construction activity, while housing starts capture construction that has begun and offer the best indication of future housing supply,” Mathieu Laberge, chief economist and senior vice-president of Housing Insights at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), previously said.

“Together, these measures show how development intentions translate into real construction activity, providing a more complete picture of the residential construction market’s trajectory.”

Kevin Hughes, CMHC’s deputy chief economist, reinforced that view: “Building permit data provides additional context for this pattern, pointing to a construction pipeline that remains subdued, in line with CMHC’s Housing Market Outlook.”

Mike Kazarian, a mortgage broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages in Toronto, Ontario, explained how the condo segment faces a prolonged recovery. 

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad. It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales,” he recently told CMP. 

Separately, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation data for September showed housing starts at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate (SAAR) of 248,896 units. That's roughly 3% above August’s figure, with the CMHC six-month moving average edging up 0.6% to 250,411 units.

items.title: B.C. home sales slide 11 per cent in October as Lower Mainland struggles
items.description:
VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year. 
 The B.C.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year. The B.C.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year.

The B.C. Real Estate Association says in a statement that the average sale price of a home in the province this October fell about 2.8 per cent from about $977,000 last year to just short of $950,000.

The latest numbers come after the association released its fourth quarter forecast this week, projecting that B.C. home sales would slide 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 to about 67,000 units.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson cites mounting market challenges from interest rates, slower immigration, oil-price shock and U.S. trade tensions, potentially contributing to the decline in the latest monthly numbers.

Ogmundson says more-affordable areas of the province have been resilient, with Kamloops seeing a 12 per cent rise in home sales last month.

But he says Metro Vancouver and the rest of the Lower Mainland continue to be hampered by "global headwinds and hawkish monetary policy," with Greater Vancouver sales falling 10 per cent to just over 2,000 units sold in October.

“Recoveries in more-expensive regions of the province are dependent on a retracing of rates and oil prices such that prospective buyers regain confidence after several volatile quarters,” Ogmundson says in the statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: Entre Nous Femmes Proposes 2-Tower Affordable Rental Project In Surrey
items.description:
Vancouver-based not-for-profit Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society is planning a new project that would add around 750 mixed-income affordable rental units to the City of Surrey, according to a new rezoning application.

Entre Nous Femmes, which is French for “Amongst us, Women,” describes itself as “one of Canada’s first women-led community housing organizations” and their mission focuses on “the unique needs of women, gender-diverse groups, single-parent families, seniors, people with disabilities, and other equity-deserving groups,” according to their website, which adds that they currently have a portfolio of 15 properties with over 700 affordable rental homes.

The site of the new Surrey project is 9883 140 Street, located about midway between 100 Avenue and the Fraser Highway, a few blocks east of the Expo Line SkyTrain’s King George Station. The site is currently occupied by an affordable housing community called Jessica Place.

According to their rezoning application, Jessica Place is currently home to 40 below-market rental townhouses, but the homes are “approaching its end of life.” The new proposal is intended to replace those units, with current residents to have the opportunity to move into the new buildings, while adding new supply.

9883 140 Street and the proposed road dedications. (WW+P Architects, Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society)

The application seeks to subdivide the site into two parcels and rezone the site to allow for one 35-storey tower and one 39-storey tower that would together deliver 748 affordable rental units. The proposal would require the Official Community Plan (OCP) designation for the site to be amended from Mid-Rise I to High-Rise I.

Phase One would be located at the centre of the site (Block 1 in the image above) and be home to the 35-storey tower, which will include 327 units. The proposed suite mix consists of 39 studio units, 147 one-bedroom units, 80 two-bedroom units, 50 three-bedroom units, and 11 four-bedroom units. The building would include 99 vehicle parking spaces, as well as some office space for the property management team.

Phase Two would then be located towards the west (Block 2) and be home to the 39-storey tower, which will include 421 units. The proposed suite mix is 42 studio units, 211 one-bedroom units, 84 two-bedroom units, 63 three-bedroom units, and 21 four-bedroom units. This building would include 167 vehicle parking spaces.

There is no Phase Three, but a small piece of the site in the northeast corner (Block 3) is intended to be consolidated with the property to the south — 9568 140 Street, a condo building — in the future. It will be used as a community garden in the interim.

The site plan for the 9883 140 Street proposal. (WW+P Architects, Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society)

According to a City planning report, Entre Nous Femmes has committed to providing all 748 units as mixed-income affordable rental units (rent-geared-to-income or low-end-of-market), but the precise affordability levels of the units are still being finalized, although a minimum of 40 units will be provided at below-market rents, replacing the existing units as required under City policy.

Amenities across the two buildings include meeting rooms, playrooms, a gymnasium, town hall room, multi-purpose rooms, co-working space, outdoor patios, playgrounds, and potentially a basketball court at the northwest corner of the site.

“The proposed development does not comply with the existing land use designation in the Official Community Plan but it does support policies in relation to increasing housing diversity and supply in areas with good access to transit and other amenities,” said City staff.

“The proposed development features high-quality architecture, appropriate site planning and an improved streetscape which benefits the overall surrounding neighbourhood. Staff support the development proposal on the subject site given that it will provide much needed mixed-income affordable rental housing within City Centre and supports the goal of achieving higher density development within close proximity to frequent transit corridors.”

One of the towers proposed for 9883 140 Street. (Entres Nous Femmes Housing Society)

On its project website, Entre Nous Femmes says all of the existing residents will gradually need to relocate temporarily as the new development will require the demolition of all the existing buildings on site. Tenants were made aware of the redevelopment plans as early as January 2025.

According to a July 2025 bulletin, the plan was to have all residents relocated by February 2027, construction commence in Summer 2027, and occupancy take place in Summer 2030, but that timeline entailed the rezoning application be approved in Summer 2026, which did not occur, so the timeline has now likely changed.

Entre Nous Femmes has submitted a rezoning application for the overall project plus a general and detailed development permit for Phase One. Earlier this week, during the first meeting of Surrey City Council following last month’s municipal elections, the associated bylaws were granted first and second readings without discussion then advanced to a public hearing scheduled for Monday, November 23.

items.title: Banks, builders urge Ottawa to ease stress test for new-home buyers
items.description: Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing
items.content: <p>Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639300957594987414.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing
items.body:
Canada’s five largest banks and a group of major homebuilders want Ottawa to loosen the mortgage stress test for first-time buyers of newly built homes.

The proposal is one of 29 recommendations in a report released this week to inform the federal review of the National Housing Strategy.

The National Housing and Investment Initiative (NHII) pairs executives from Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Royal Bank of Canada, Scotiabank and Toronto-Dominion Bank with developers including Mattamy Homes and Minto Group.

Its central argument is that homes built for ownership will not get built unless buyers can qualify for financing.

How the stress test could change for first-time buyers

The group wants a sliding minimum qualifying rate tied to mortgage term and buyer type. It would set a softer test for first-time buyers of new construction, for example qualifying them at the contract rate plus 1.5 percentage points rather than two.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) is leaving the stress test unchanged, keeping qualification at 5.25% or two points above a borrower’s contract rate, whichever is higher, after it reviewed its mortgage stress test rules in January.

The report also calls for a federal down payment assistance program limited to new homes. 

“The current stress test is a valuable prudential tool but may be too blunt an instrument by excluding otherwise creditworthy borrowers,” the report said.

The coalition acknowledged the trade-off. “However, there are concerns that loosening the rules could, among other things, cause a spike in resale home prices and harm affordability,” the report said.

It argued that limiting relief to newly built homes would keep that pressure off the resale market.

Foreign buyer and condo asks meet a slumping new-build market

The report names five priorities:

  1. a permanent version of Ontario’s enhanced harmonized sales tax (HST) rebate
  2. a capital gains rollover, modelled on the US Section 1031 provision, for investors who reinvest proceeds in purpose-built rentals
  3. alternatives to development charges
  4. a foreign buyer ban exemption for new construction
  5. an Owner-Occupied Construction Loan Program for condominiums

Ottawa has already acted on one of them. Its 2026 budget kept the foreign buyer ban but loosened its terms to exclude newly built properties.

Joel Fox, co-founder and chief operating officer of Ownright, warned Canadian Mortgage Professional of the risk that those places just sit empty. 

Joel Fox of Ownright says allowing foreign buyers to purchase newly built homes could support new construction and housing supply, while continued restrictions on resale properties help address concerns around speculation. https://t.co/mkrwdSPIxq — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

The report says the HST reforms helped sell about 5,000 additional homes in the program’s first three months.

Micky Khaneka of MKG Mortgages in Toronto said Ontario’s temporary HST rebate on new homes “has sparked some renewed interest in the newer homes, especially new builds.” 

Condos remain the weak spot. According to the report, condos have historically supplied upwards of 40% of Canada’s urban housing stock, yet they have no equivalent to the $55-billion Apartment Construction Loan Program for rentals.

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad,” Mike Kazarian, a Toronto broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages, told CMP this week. 

“It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales.”

Brad Carr, CEO, Canada, at Mattamy Homes and NHII co-chair, said the country’s goals “will require a significant expansion of the development pipeline, greater access to long-term capital, modernized financial regulation, predictable immigration policies and access to better data to support all of those decisions.”

items.title: Industry leaders urge new B.C. government to revisit housing policies
items.description: Real estate industry groups want tax changes, lower construction costs to revive housing development
items._ogDesc: Real estate industry groups want tax changes, lower construction costs to revive housing development
items.body:
People in B.C.’s real estate industry are urging the incoming provincial government to revisit housing policies in an effort to revive the province’s housing market.

Groups representing developers and real estate agents say the government should assess existing policies and determine which ones to modify or scrap, as well as consider introducing new measures to reduce construction costs and encourage more housing development.

“We have a cost of delivery crisis. It costs more to build than what people can afford,” said Michael Drummond, CEO of the Urban Development Institute (UDI).

Metro Vancouver’s new condo construction saw a 15-year low in the first half of 2026, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), highlighting weak presales and high construction costs.

“So effectively when the current amount of housing is sold, there is no next new project,” said Drummond. “When immigration normalizes, we're going to get another spike in prices.”

Drummond said he hopes the BC Conservatives will revisit policies introduced by the previous NDP government that could potentially add to construction costs. He said he wants the government to pause mandatory increases to the BC Energy Step Code and Zero Carbon Step Code.

The former BC Liberak introduced the BC Energy Step Code in 2017 to gradually improve energy efficiency in new buildings, and the Zero Carbon Step Code in 2023 to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from new buildings. He wants the government to pause mandatory increases to the BC Energy Step Code and Zero Carbon Step Code.

For large buildings, the province currently requires Step 2 of the Energy Step Code, meaning new construction must be about 20 per cent more energy efficient than required under the previous building standards. Higher steps require greater energy efficiency.

Drummond wants the provincial minimum for large buildings held at Step 2.

UDI is also urging the incoming Conservative government to cancel PST expansion to professional services and introduce a development charge reduction program modelled on Ontario’s recent approach.

“The previous government tried to rely on demand-side measures, they've tried to rely on taxes, and a tax never built a new home,” said Drummond.

The BC Real Estate Association (BCREA) is also asking the Conservative government to review the Step Code and home-energy policies, halt the planned PST expansion, and reconsider housing-related taxes, including the Speculation and Vacancy Tax introduced in 2018. The association argues that these measures add to the tax burden and the costs of purchasing a home.

“Over the last several years, we haven't exactly had a shortage of housing policy,” said Jasroop Gosal, the BCREA’s government relations manager.

Gosal pointed to the introduction of Bills 44 and 47, changes to development financing and the Energy Step Code, the Speculation and Vacancy tax, the home-flipping tax, the foreign buyer tax, housing targets and affordable housing programs.

“And the list goes on and on and on. So the question now is: what happens to all of that when governments change?”

BCREA is calling on the new government to establish a permanent Provincial Housing Policy Roundtable, bringing together different stakeholders from across B.C.’s real estate industry to review existing housing policies, as a first step.

How to measure success?

Industry leaders say they don’t expect the new government to solve the housing problem right away, but there are certain changes they hope to see within a year.

“One year is not very long when it comes to housing because of the development pipeline,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the BC Non-Profit Housing Association.

She said the industry wants to see more clarity about the government’s direction and the tools it is prepared to use, something she said has been missing for the last couple of years.

“If in one year the entire housing ecosystem understood with clarity the direction that the government wants to go, what tools it's prepared to use, and the level of investment it's required to make into affordability for British Columbians … that would be helpful to the whole sector,” she said.

“That provides the predictability where you then have the sector investing in the pre-development process. That investment can't happen if there's uncertainty in the regulatory or the provincial government or any government environment.”

Gosal said he thinks success would include the government launching the housing roundtable and beginning work on the policies that “will make the biggest impact today.”

“And that priority will be set by not only the provincial government, but also the roundtable participants,” he said.

“The outcome [should] be: you would start to see movement in the housing sector, in the development sector, more activity, pre-sales actually starting to be sold, movement in the construction of housing.”

Success would also mean reducing enough costs to make housing more affordable to build, according to Drummond.

“When we get enough costs out of the system, [then] we can deliver a unit for the wages that people make in British Columbia,” he said.

items.title: Toronto condo market recovery could still be 'two to three years' away
items.description: The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027
items.content: <p>The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639300218631918153.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027
items.body:
Mortgage and housing market watchers have been waiting for years for Toronto’s beleaguered condo sector to finally gather pace – but a 2027 recovery doesn’t look to be in the cards as buyers continue to snub the space.

October saw yet another decline in condo sales and prices, and while many mortgage brokers working in the city see some opportunities for buyers among other property types, the familiar problems plaguing the condo market seem likely to persist.

Mike Kazarian (pictured top), a Toronto-based mortgage broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages, told Canadian Mortgage Professional he’s still been hearing of potential condo buyers facing financing challenges – and he doesn’t expect the market to see any improvement when 2027 comes around.

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad,” he said. “It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales.”

A new federal government initiative to accelerate permanent residency for workers already living in Canada has changed the immigration picture slightly over the past week, although RBC Economics doesn’t see the change having a significant impact on housing – for now.

“Given the abundance of inventory in the housing market, a modest acceleration in population growth doesn’t introduce substantial risk to affordability near-term,” RBC economist Rachel Battaglia said in a report this week. “That said, this could quickly change as existing pent-up demand is unlocked.”

While end users and first-time buyers are still avoiding the condo sector, recent months have seen some interest emerge among bigger investors including Jesta Group, a global real estate firm that reportedly earmarked $500 million worth of Toronto condos for investment earlier this year.

Kazarian said he sees that trend continuing. “I think you’re going to see a lot of REITS [real estate investment trusts] and big companies come in and buy these condos for purpose-built rentals,” he said.

“And look, we need rentals in the city. We need to make it more affordable, but that’s not going to help out the mortgage business and people looking to buy.”

Lower prices could spark a better homebuying outlook elsewhere

One possible bright spot for the condo sector: the federal government’s recent announcement that it intends to amend the ban on non-resident foreign buyers, extending that restriction into 2029 but loosening it to exclude the purchase of newbuild homes.

Some analysts say that decision could open the door to foreign investment in the preconstruction sector, potentially putting a floor under the market’s years-long correction.

Still, it remains to be seen whether that drums up enough interest to get the market moving again – especially for microunits, the now-notorious sub-500-square-foot condos built for renting but seeing little to no interest among potential buyers who want to live in the property they purchase.

Prices have been sliding across the board in Toronto, and outside the condo sector Kazarian said he sees reason to believe homebuyers will continue to snag deals and find the right purchasing opportunity in 2027.

“I think a lot of people are going to be cautious [next year], but on the flipside of that housing prices re coming down. We’ve seen, across the GTA [Greater Toronto Area], an approximately 21% decrease in housing prices [since their 2022 peak]. So is now a good time to buy? It might be.”

Trade, inflation concerns linger as 2027 nears

Other clouds are continuing to hover over the housing outlook, though – including trade tensions with the US and the continuing US-Iran war, both of which have sparked economic fears.

The Iran war has pushed up fuel prices and raised fears of Bank of Canada rate increases caused by inflation pressure, while the ongoing trade turmoil has spiked concerns about job losses and layoffs in tariff-impacted areas.

The issue of job security is one that frequently rears its head with customers, according to Kazarian. “I’ve seen many clients where they’ll take the position that they want to make sure they can quality for the mortgage based on one income versus both because they’re just being cautious in the event that one of them loses their job,” he said.

“So I think the market will pick up, but people are going to be cautious and they’re going to be selective. I don’t think we’re going to see any kind of multiple offer situations, but I think it might be a good time to buy.”

items.title: Could an immigration surge boost Canada's 2027 mortgage demand?
items.description: A new immigration ceiling could accelerate Canada housing demand recovery as newcomer pipeline grows
items.content: <p>A new immigration ceiling could accelerate Canada housing demand recovery as newcomer pipeline grows</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638542251211658290.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new immigration ceiling could accelerate Canada housing demand recovery as newcomer pipeline grows
items.body:
Canada’s housing demand may face new pressure in 2027 as immigration measures create conditions for a record number of permanent resident admissions. 

Analysis from RBC Economics finds that overlapping one-time exemptions could push Canada’s permanent resident (PR) admissions ceiling to 662,000 next year. Those exemptions are stacked across two consecutive immigration plans.  

That figure is the highest annual intake on record, far above the government’s official 380,000 PR target. For mortgage brokers already managing tight affordability conditions and elevated inventory, the question is how quickly the market could tighten again.   

What’s driving the spike? 

The government’s official target remains at 380,000 new permanent residents every year. Last year’s immigration plan included exemptions for up to 115,000 protected persons and their dependents. It also covered 33,000 skilled workers already in Canada across 2026 and 2027.   

Based on updated 2026 allocations, 82,000 of those admissions are expected to carry into 2027. The latest plan layers an additional 200,000 transitions on top, bringing RBC Economics’ derived total ceiling to 662,000.   

Ottawa’s stated aim is to reduce the 2.7 million non-permanent residents (NPRs) currently in Canada, targeting a population share closer to 5%. The new exemptions are designed to accelerate that transition by converting temporary residents already in the country to permanent residency.  

Will the NPR drawdown actually happen? 

Whether this produces a population boom or a neutral reshuffle depends on one critical question. Will temporary residents who gain permanent status represent net new people in the country?   

RBC Economics notes that roughly 200,000 NPRs transition to permanent residency annually. If the 200,000 new exemption spaces are filled by people who would have left Canada regardless, the population impact is limited. But if even a portion of those transitions retain individuals who would otherwise have departed, population growth accelerates beyond official projections.  

The historical record is not encouraging for the drawdown scenario. The 2024 Levels Plan targeted a significant reduction in the NPR population through departures and transitions.   

By end of 2025, the actual outflow had closed only about half the gap against target, according to RBC Economics. The shortfall has continued through 2026. Statistics Canada issued a significant upward revision to its national population estimate earlier this year, driven by the NPR base coming in well above projections.   

What does the 2027 surge mean for Canada’s housing demand? 

RBC Economics argues the current inventory overhang limits immediate affordability risk. That cushion is not permanent — a sustained population pickup would begin absorbing supply faster than new listings can replace it.   

For brokers, the more immediate signal is on the demand side. The plan lowers barriers for high-earning applicants already in Canada.   

It reduces point thresholds, boosts points for high-wage workers, and eliminates the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) requirement for certain categories. Recent Statistics Canada data show that economic-class immigrants are entering the ownership market faster than earlier cohorts despite affordability challenges. That signals this cohort converts to mortgage clients relatively quickly.   

That profile of applicants — employed, higher-income, already settled in Canada — tend to be mortgage-ready sooner than a new arrival. A population acceleration in 2027, even a modest one, shifts that dynamic. First-time buyer demand, already pent up after years of affordability challenges, could return more sharply than current forecasts suggest.  

The 2027 ceiling reverts to 380,000 from 2028 onward. But returning to that figure after a record year still requires a drawdown of the transitional cohort. The government’s track record on hitting NPR reduction targets suggests that won’t happen automatically.   

What should brokers be watching? 

Brokers tracking Canada’s immigration policy will want to monitor whether the NPR population share falls as intended. Even if the government doubles NPR-to-PR transitions next year, RBC Economics projects Canada is unlikely to hit the 5% share target in 2027.  

Statistics Canada confirmed a third consecutive quarterly population contraction in early 2026 — a trend that illustrates how quickly Canada housing demand can reverse.   

The plan does not extend beyond 2027. But the downstream effects on inventory absorption, first-home buyer competition, and mortgage origination volumes could persist well into 2028 and 2029. Canada’s mortgage professionals are already operating in territory without demographic precedent. Canada housing demand projections remain volatile enough that brokers should be stress-testing their pipelines now.

items._ogDesc: Lender's Q3 results show $24 billion under administration as originations outpace last year
items.body:
RFA Financial's Q3 financials, released this week, showed the company put mortgages under administration at $24 billion, with on- and off-balance sheet originations continuing to climb.

The company's lending operations run through two subsidiaries: RFA Mortgage Corporation for prime residential lending, and RFA Bank of Canada for alternative mortgages. RFA Bank is a federally regulated Schedule I bank.

The numbers signal a lender expanding across both prime and alternative segments. Credit metrics remain well inside industry norms.

What's driving RFA Financial’s Q3 origination growth?

The bulk of Q3 activity flowed through broker and partner channels, which RFA describes as central to its underwriting model. Through those channels, $1.5 billion in mortgages were placed with third parties or securitized during the quarter. On-balance sheet originations added a further $198.5 million.

According to RFA’s Q3 2026 investor presentation, year-to-date originations grew 31% compared with the same period in 2025. Ben Rodney, president and chief executive officer of RFA Financial Inc., said in the November 10 press release: “Mortgage origination growth continues to exceed last year’s volumes and ongoing dispositions at sale prices above IFRS values demonstrate the disciplined execution of our transitional strategy.”

RFA’s first-quarter 2026 results had already signalled that momentum was building. The company reported over $1 billion in originations in that quarter alone.

2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026* $0.01B $0.32B $2.5B $3.2B $3.1B $2.8B $4.1B $5.4B $5.2B* Full-year total 2026 YTD (Jan–Sept) — not comparable to full-year figures Source: RFA Financial Inc. Q3 2026 investor presentation, November 11, 2026  ·  * 2026 figure is year-to-date to September 30, 2026  ·  2018–2019 figures exclude Street Capital originations prior to its Q4 2019 acquisition   Net interest income for the quarter was $18 million. The adjusted net interest margin — stripping out non-cash purchase price adjustments from the company’s February 2026 reverse acquisition — was 2.4%.

Pre-provision pre-tax income, a measure of core operating profitability before credit loss provisions, came in at $7.6 million for the quarter.

The company continued selling real estate assets from its February 2026 reverse acquisition. By September 30, RFA had closed property sales totalling $264.8 million year to date. The strategy is designed to rotate capital into the financial services platform. A lender redirecting capital into lending assets carries more capacity to fund new originations.

The pace of that rotation became clearer in Q3. RFA signed a 20-year lease with IG Wealth Management at two Winnipeg office properties, pushing committed occupancy from 79.6% to around 95.1%. Net rental income in that portfolio is expected to rise by around 59.7% as a result.

RFA Financial’s Q3 trajectory points to a lender in scale-up mode. Origination growth, a borrower credit score of 699, and a CET1 ratio of 16.09% each tell part of the story.

The post Canadian Housing Affordability’s Record Recovery May End Soon: NBF appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian housing affordability improved for a record 11 quarters, but homes remain unaffordable and rising mortgage rates threaten further gains, warns NBF.
items.body:
Canadian real estate affordability just saw its longest improvement streak in history. National Bank‘s Q3 housing affordability index shows a record 11 quarters of improvements. Tragically, a long streak of minor improvements means it’s still one of the worst markets ever. The bank warns that higher mortgage rates are also likely to bring those improvements to an end.

Canadian Housing Affordability Improves For Longest Streak Ever

Monthly mortgage payment on median home price, all types of dwellings (25-year amortization, 5-year term)

Source: National Bank Financial.

Canadian housing affordability just printed its longest improvement streak ever. Mortgage payments on a typical home as a share of median household income fell 0.7 percentage points to 50.9% in Q3 2026. That means a household would spend 50.9 cents of every pre-tax dollar they make to pay a mortgage at today’s prices. While high, that’s the lowest it’s been in a while.

“Housing affordability improved for an eleventh consecutive quarter in Q3 2026, extending the longest period of gains on record,” explains National Bank economist Kyle Dahms.

The improvement was driven by lower home prices and higher incomes. A 1.0% drop in seasonally adjusted home prices in Q3 trimmed 0.5 points from the index. At the same time, the bank estimates that household income rose 0.7% in the quarter, trimming 0.4 points from the index. Together, those gains more than covered the 0.2-point erosion from rising mortgage rates in the quarter.

Affordability improved due to falling prices and higher incomes, not cheaper financing? Fascinating, but let’s put a pin in that for a moment.

Canada’s Record Affordability Gains Still Leave Housing Unaffordable

Despite the streak, actually buying a home is pretty much impossible for most of Canada. After peaking at roughly 66% of income in 2023, the index has made a sharp improvement. “The cumulative improvement since Q4 2023 now approaches 15 percentage points, although the Composite 10 remains 9.7 points above its historical average and 8.5 points higher than its pre-pandemic level,” explains Dahms.

Keep in mind that longer elevation above the average since 2000 helps to drag that number higher. Ten years ago, the average since 2000 was 31.1% of income, according to the bank’s report from then. It’s since climbed to 41.2%, meaning the baseline is worse and normalizing the lack of affordability.

That said, the bank warns this may be as good as it gets in the near term.

Soaring Mortgage Rates Threaten To Derail Improvements

Rising mortgage rates threaten to offset affordability gains. The bank’s 5-year fixed benchmark mortgage rate added 38 basis points (bps) in October, up 45 bps from its Q3 average. It was the largest monthly jump in four years, pushing the rate to its highest level since July 2024.

“All in all, housing affordability is facing in Q4 its most significant interest-rate challenge since 2022,” warns Dahms.

If home prices are flat in October, mortgage rates would add 2.4 points to the payment burden. That would be partially offset by a 0.2-point improvement from rising incomes, but still leave the index at 53.1%. What happens is anyone’s guess for the rest of the year, but the Bank of Canada (BoC) sees this continuing. The central bank warns inflation won’t return to the target rate until 2028. That’s a long return trip with higher borrowing costs along the way.

While the bank’s view is that higher rates will erode affordability, they don’t touch the outlook beyond Q4. In this very Q3 report, affordability improved alongside higher rates. Rising mortgage rates diminish credit capacity, reducing household leverage and thus liquidity. Weaker liquidity pushes prices lower, which can potentially offset the pain over time.

BoC research previously revealed that home prices absorbed savings from lower interest rates. Instead of saving on interest, prices rose to absorb the extra debt service capacity. The US Federal Reserve made a similar argument, while the BIS attributes the post-pandemic global home price surge to rates being too low for too long.
