items._ogDesc: Stellantis has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years.
items.body:
Stellantis has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years.

From retooling plans to the facility being sold, it’s been a wild few years for the plant, which has now come to a head as Unifor and government officials criticize Stellantis’ deal with Roshel while the companies argue it’s the way forward if jobs are to return to the factory.

  • Carney government actively involved in talks leading to Stellantis plant sale: sources

Here’s a timeline of the key events leading up to Roshel buying the Stellantis plant:

December 2023: Stellantis idles the Brampton plant to begin retooling for the production of the Jeep Compass electric SUV. More than 2,200 Unifor Local 1285 workers are laid off.

Retooling begins in January 2024 to prepare for the Jeep Compass, but after U.S. President Donald Trump starts rolling out tariffs in 2025, the company halts that work.

2025

Oct. 14: Stellantis says the production previously earmarked for its Brampton assembly plant is being moved to Illinois. The move is part of a US$13-billion plan by the American automaker to expand U.S. production by 50 per cent over the next four years.

Oct. 15: Unifor, which represents the workers, along with Canadian politicians, call on Stellantis to fulfil commitments it made to workers. Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the company has a duty to live up to its promises to workers, while Prime Minister Mark Carney says the move is a direct consequence of the latest U.S. tariffs.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly later expresses “extreme concern” about the move in a letter to the company, where she threatens legal action. She says the company had agreed to maintain its full Canadian footprint, including Brampton operations, in exchange for substantial financial support over decades — referring to 2009 government bailouts of the auto sector during the financial crisis.

Oct. 16: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he was told by the global head of Stellantis that the automaker is looking for a new model for the Brampton plant, but more trade certainty is needed to make any decision.

Nov. 3: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Ottawa is launching a dispute resolution process against Stellantis over its decision to move production to the U.S. Joly tells a House of Commons committee she sent the company a letter informing it that Ottawa was initiating the formal, 30-day settlement process to “recover” taxpayer funds and “bring back production” to the facility.

Dec. 4: Joly says Canada is serving Stellantis a notice of default of its federal contracts after shifting some production to the U.S.

2026

Aug. 14: Unifor says Stellantis is seriously considering the closure and sale of the assembly plant.

Sept. 1: Unifor and Stellantis begin contract talks, with the potential plant sale looming over discussions.

Sept. 11: Stellantis says it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel to sell the plant. Unifor pauses contract talks, citing an impasse over the future of the plant, and later urges the federal government to intervene in the sale.

Sept. 17: Unifor says a strike is a “real possibility” after labour negotiations break down.

Oct. 19: Stellantis workers in Canada vote 97.3 per cent in favour of a strike mandate.

Nov. 6: Unifor says it believes Stellantis had sold its idled assembly plant. The company does not confirm nor deny whether a sale had been finalized.

Nov. 9: Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with Roshel for the plant. Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and associated equipment for an undisclosed amount.

Unifor national president Lana Payne says in a press conference that the automaker has betrayed union members with an “underhanded deal” that walks away from its commitments to workers at the plant.

Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov fires back at critics, defending the deal as “the best thing that can happen to this plant and to this city.”

He says he’s surprised the government hasn’t publicly supported the sale given his company’s intention of creating thousands of jobs at the idled facility.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

items.description: New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market
items.content: <p>New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/035/0365_639299607476918333.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market
items.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is set to create more jobs than it eliminates by the end of the decade, according to new forecasts from Gartner.

The business and technology insights company projects that AI will generate 10.6 million new jobs and remove 8.9 million by 2030, a net increase of 1.7 million positions.

Gartner also broke down the expected impact of AI on jobs across three types of industries.

In asset-intensive industries, Gartner expects AI to create 6.4 million jobs and eliminate six million by 2030. AI-driven job losses are projected to affect 0.4% of the sector's workforce.

These industries, which deal in physical products or deliver services within capital-intensive physical infrastructure, account for the largest share of jobs globally.

The technology sector is heavily affected by AI, with nearly 70% of its workforce highly exposed. Even so, Gartner expects the sector to create 1.9 million jobs and lose 0.4 million by 2030. AI job losses are projected to represent 1.8% of the global technology workforce over the period.

The public sector is the only one of the three where Gartner forecasts more jobs lost than gained: 0.9 million losses against 0.4 million gains by 2030.

AI-driven job losses are projected to total 0.4% of the global public sector workforce. Gartner added that AI investment in the sector is unlikely to be enough to offset severe future skills shortages driven by other factors.

Gartner's findings come amid worker fears that AI will wipe out jobs. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push US unemployment to between 10 and 20% in the next one to five years.

But Helen Poitevin, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, said the organisations furthest along with AI are using it to rethink how they operate, not simply to cut staff.

"Organisations most advanced in AI execution view AI not as a replacement for labour, but as a catalyst to reinvent operations and rebalance workforce and technology capabilities to compete in changing markets. They ensure AI's economic value goes beyond replacing labour," Poitevin said at the Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo in Barcelona.

Hiring put on hold

Despite the positive overall outlook, Gartner's forecast points to a less visible effect of AI on the labour market: roles that are never created.

According to Gartner, one of the most significant impacts on the job market in 2026 was executives' decisions to defer the creation and hiring of 1.3 million positions. Gartner's 2026 figures also show 2.2 million jobs lost and 1.6 million gained.

By 2030, Gartner expects five million people to have experienced delayed hiring as business and IT executives postpone the creation of new positions.

"Deferred jobs are not the same as lost jobs. They simply aren't created," said John Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst, Chief of Research at Gartner.

Job losses limited, transformation widespread

Gartner projects that between 0.4 and 1.8% of workers will experience job loss directly attributable to AI by 2030.

Far more workers will see their roles change. Gartner estimates that just over 20% of workers, or 435.5 million employees, will have to adapt to the new shape of work through 2030. That includes changes to what they do, how they do it and where their responsibilities begin and end.

Poitevin warned employers against assuming AI will affect every part of their business in the same way.

"AI job impacts are unevenly distributed across geographies, job functions and industries. The worst mistake that a business and IT executive can make is to apply lessons from one industry or role to another which can lead to poor errors in judgement and missed targets," she said.

"Each industry faces unique challenges and risks that executive leaders must understand and address."

items.title: Insider: Developers Still Need Someone To Write The Equity Cheque
items.description:
A better loan offer won't get a stalled project built if nobody is willing to put up the equity.

That problem runs through PwC and the Urban Land Institute's Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027. Among Canadian survey respondents, 63% expect equity for development and redevelopment to be undersupplied in 2027. For debt, the figure is 46%. These are views on capital availability, not financing rejection rates. Even so, they put a limit on how much optimism developers should take from a recovery in dealmaking.

Cheaper or more available debt helps. The developer still needs an investor willing to fund the rest.

Canadian respondents were more likely to expect an undersupply of development/redevelopment equity capital (63%) than debt capital (46%) in 2027. These are survey expectations, not measured financing volumes. Source: PwC and ULI, Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027, pp. 136–137. Original chart.

More deals do not necessarily mean more construction

Canadian commercial real estate investment reached $16.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026, according to the CBRE figures cited in the report. That was the strongest quarter since early 2022. The total includes mergers and acquisitions, so a few large transactions can do a lot of the lifting. It tells us money is moving again, without telling us how broadly the recovery has spread.

There is also a practical reason an investor might buy an existing building before funding a new one. An occupied property already collects rent. A development can spend years consuming cash before the first tenant moves in.

The buyer of an existing building can negotiate the price down. A developer has to work with the cost of delivering a new one. Construction and servicing bills don't fall just because the building down the street sold at a discount.

That leaves room for a busy acquisitions market and a weak construction market at the same time. Investors can buy assets from struggling owners without financing the next round of projects.

Some of those sales will help. A new owner may have the cash to finish a stalled building, or a lower purchase price may finally make the numbers work. The test is whether construction follows the transaction.

Toronto is already starting fewer homes

The report puts Toronto census metropolitan area housing starts at 26,087 in 2025, down from 37,718 in 2024, citing CMHC. That is 11,631 fewer homes started in a year, a decline of about 31%. These are historical construction starts, not a prediction of how many homes will be finished in 2027.

Toronto census metropolitan area housing starts fell from 37,718 units in 2024 to 26,087 in 2025, a 30.8% decline (rounded to 31%). Starts measure construction begun, not completed homes. Source: CMHC, as cited in PwC and ULI, Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027, p. 145. Original chart.

A thinner construction pipeline gives developers a reason to expect less competition when their buildings open. It can be a sound argument for buying a site. It is a much harder argument to make to an investor who needs their money back before the project is ready.

In the meantime, the carrying costs keep coming.

A partner willing to wait through a slow lease-up gives a project more room than one counting on an early sale. Both can believe Toronto needs more housing. They still need to agree on how long they can afford to wait for the income.

A rental conversion needs a new business plan

The report describes continued long-term interest in purpose-built rental. Some interviewees are much less convinced that today's rents can cover the cost of building and financing it. Both views can be reasonable.

Changing a condo proposal to rental means rewriting the business plan. The developer gives up the expected proceeds from individual suite sales and collects rent over years instead. The design and financing have to support that longer commitment, including the cost of running the building.

Start with the rent a tenant will actually pay. If a competing building offers free months, its advertised rent overstates what the landlord collects over that lease. Using that advertised rent as a comparable can overstate the income the new project will collect.

Then check how long it will take to fill the building. Reaching the target rent six months late can still leave the owner short of cash. The partners need to know who covers that shortfall before the first bill arrives.

The next equity cheque may go into an old building

Loans coming due in 2027 will compete for that money too. PwC and ULI describe owners using preferred equity, mezzanine financing and joint ventures to close funding gaps.

If a replacement loan is smaller than the debt being repaid, the borrower has to make up the difference. That can mean putting cash into a building they already own instead of buying the next site.

The terms deserve as much attention as the amount raised. Preferred returns and fees can leave less income for the original owner. Repayment deadlines can force decisions well before that owner intended to sell. A refinancing that solves today's shortage may leave very little room for the next delay.

Before committing more money, a developer should know which assumption the project can least afford to get wrong. If a small rent reduction or a few extra months of vacancy wipes out the return, a higher exit value in the spreadsheet is doing too much work.

Housing policy has to deal with those gaps too. A fee reduction helps if it brings the cost within reach of the revenue a project can earn. A financing program helps if it supplies money on terms the project can carry. The evidence of success is a financed project that starts construction.

The report gives developers a reason to call investors again. Those calls still have to end with an agreement on the equity and how long it can stay in the project. Until then, a recovery in transactions offers limited comfort to the owner paying to hold an empty site.

items._ogDesc: OTTAWA — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.

The budget, which was tabled last week, dropped any mention of that original target, which was introduced in the Liberals' 2025 election platform and repeated numerous times in that year's budget.

Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built, but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson's office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.

After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still "working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade."

At the time, The Canadian Press had asked Robertson's office about Ottawa's commitment to the target because April's spring economic update also lacked references to the goal.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government's fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, "no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided."

Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.

On Tuesday, Robertson's office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.

"Since forming government, we launched an ambitious national plan to focus our efforts and spur co-ordinated action between governments, homebuilders, and communities. We moved quickly to increase housing supply and improve access to safe, warm, affordable homes," his office said.

MP Scott Aitchison, the Conservative housing critic, accused the Liberals of quietly dropping the promise to double home building and replacing it with the smaller non-market target.

"Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability," Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.

"Canadians need homes they can afford, not more failed Liberal targets and broken promises.”

In its fall housing supply report, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. wrote that the country is entering a "new phase" where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The CMHC's "business-as-usual" forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the CMHC said.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, said he always viewed the Liberals' goal of doubling home building levels as a tough one to achieve. It would mean bringing the annual number of housing starts up to 500,000 in a given year, when Canada has so far topped out around 300,000.

Moffatt said the target may also be "excessive," given that the government can effectively control the pace of population growth, which dictates how much supply is really needed to serve the Canadian market.

The headline number also doesn't specify what kinds of homes Canada needs to build to actually meet Canadians' needs, he added.

"I never loved the target. I felt it was probably too high and missed some important nuances," Moffatt said.

The federal Liberals have instituted a number of policy changes aimed at stimulating home building since Prime Minister Mark Carney came to office in March 2025.

They include waiving the GST on many newly built homes, establishing new funds for local infrastructure and setting up Build Canada Homes, a new Crown corporation tasked with reversing years of lagging non-market home construction.

Budget 2026 proposed giving another $13 billion over 10 years to Build Canada Homes and pledged tens of billions of dollars over the coming decade to an effort to end homelessness across the country.

Andy Yan, director of the City Program at Simon Fraser University, also said he considered Ottawa's original home building goal "more aspirational than realistic."

"You can set a target, but do you have the capacity to meet those targets?" he said.

Yan said policies like the Housing Accelerator Fund and the Apartment Construction Loan Program have been "fairly successful" in getting more homes built, particularly on the rental side.

The Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties federal cash to pro-development policy changes, was one of Ottawa's tools for addressing the fact that barriers to building often lie at the municipal level.

Many of the other levers for stimulating home building are also not directly in the federal government's hands.

Building material costs have grown in response to U.S. tariffs, while a soft labour market is dampening buyer demand for new homes.

Interest rates — a critical factor for developers weighing the business case for a new build — are set independently by the Bank of Canada. The central bank delivered its first rate hike in more than three years last month and signalled more could be on the way.

Moffatt warned that many of the constraints holding back broader construction apply to social housing as well.

"There's no non-market drywall, right? There's no non-market lumber, there's no non market electrician," he said.

"A non-market social housing target is more in the government's control, but it's hardly a slam dunk."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: BMO sees Canada’s immigration changes doubling expected population growth in 2027, keeping housing demand higher as more temporary residents stay.
items.body:
Canada’s continuing its immigration experiments but this time it’s a little more discreet. Ottawa’s 2027-29 immigration plan maintains the current regular permanent resident admissions target. However, BMO notes that existing and new special measures mean the number of permanent residents will be much higher. As a result, the bank’s economists have nearly doubled their population growth forecast.

Canada’s Immigration Measures Lift Effective Target To 660,000

Ottawa’s immigration target may look conservative, but it’s much bigger than the fragmented announcements suggest. The 2027-2029 immigration plan maintains 380,000 admissions annually, but BMO projects the target is actually much higher than the headline numbers suggest.

“While Ottawa maintains permanent resident targets of 380k per year, special one-time measures (from both the 2025 and 2026 budgets) build significantly on that amount,” explains BMO senior economist Robert Kavcic.

Canada Hopes To Attract A Lot More Permanent Residents

Permanent residents: actual admissions, target admissions, and special measures.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; StatCan; Budget 2026.

He notes that special measures in Budget 2025 and 2026 add roughly 280,000 temporary-to-permanent resident transitions in 2027. “In other words, roughly 280k temporary residents will be granted permanent resident status in 2027, with officials suggesting this will be on top of new admissions,” says Kavcic. After the special measures, BMO puts the total closer to 660,000 permanent residents.

BMO Sees Population Growth Rebounding To Nearly 1% In 2027

The measures mean population growth is seen bouncing much higher than previously forecast. BMO now expects the population to expand roughly 1% in 2027, nearly double the 0.5% they previously anticipated. “In effect, because those temporary residents are now not leaving, they will not drag on population growth as previously expected,” explains Kavcic.

The special measures largely aim to keep people already in the country. Converting their status won’t immediately add housing demand, but fewer departures would mean fewer homes freed up for the temporary resident inflow. This reduced churn can boost housing demand more than previously anticipated, even without changing the headline immigration target.

“This is an abrupt change in the near-term outlook,” says Kavcic, questioning whether repeated one-time measures make planning harder for the Bank of Canada, homebuilders, and municipalities.

Since housing takes years to build, the read is that policymakers are trying to overshoot supply with further demand stimulus. However, the state of the Canadian economy is very different from last time it was attempted. With Canadians leaving in record volumes to find opportunities elsewhere, the ability to retain and attract immigrants may be harder than simply raising a quota.

items.title: What brokers need to know about an ever-evolving appraisal process
items.description: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.content: <p>Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639299368595742752.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.body:
Canadian mortgage brokers have established themselves as a key conduit between borrowers and lenders – but in the alternative lending space, that role expands to becoming the connector between borrower, lender, and appraiser.

That fact means it’s doubly important for brokers in the sector to take the time to understand what appraisers do and why they do it, according to Appraisal Institute of Canada (AIC) director Claudio Polito (pictured top). 

Among the main misconceptions about an appraiser’s role, Polito told Canadian Mortgage Professional, is that an appraisal is simply a property value. “To most people – the borrower, the broker, perhaps even the lender – the value is the most important part,” he said. “But to the appraiser, the value is just a component of it. There’s a story to be told.”

That story includes neighbourhood context, physical improvements, and market activity – all of which feed into the final opinion of value. Polito also pointed out that lender requirements vary considerably, and brokers should factor this into their preparation.

“Brokers are asked to know their client and we’re asking them to know their lender as well,” he said. “A Big Five bank may have one requirement. A private lending individual may have a different requirement. Even within the same space, there are different requirements.”

Polito’s main advice for brokers is on client preparation, an area he said too many brokers overlook until problems arise. His recommendation: get ahead of potential issues by asking the right questions early.

“Rather than having the appraiser highlight potential areas of concern, have the broker be made aware of that first,” he said. “Do you have a basement apartment? Is it registered? Is it approved by the municipality? Do you have an addition? Was it done with or without permits? These are questions the appraiser will ask – better we know up front.”

What’s changed in the current market

In the current climate, expectation management on value is equally important – especially because of the significant drop in values across many markets since the peak of 2021 and 2022. The borrowers who purchased at the height of the market sometimes carry expectations that no longer reflect reality, according to Polito.

“If you purchased your property in Toronto in 2022 for $1 million and you’re asking for a home line of credit and thinking the property is worth $1.5 million, what makes you think the property has gone up half a million dollars when everything in the news says the Toronto market is declining?” he said.

The condo market has suffered an especially noteworthy downturn, leading to appraisal challenges as buyers who purchased preconstruction units are suddenly unable to secure a mortgage for the amount they agreed to buy the property for years back.

How AI is impacting the appraisal process

Another big trend to impact the appraisals space in recent years, unsurprisingly, has been artificial intelligence (AI). The rise of AI-driven property valuations is having a big say on how some borrowers, and even some lenders, approach the question of what a property is worth.

Polito still believes AI will never completely eradicate the human influence from the appraisal process. “AI can be a great tool when it’s properly applied with guardrails in place, when there’s the human element and the human involvement in it,” he said.

“But you’re seeing more and more homeowners and borrowers relying on AI – and that could be dangerous. It could lead to false expectations, either overstated or understated.”

On automated valuation models (AVMs), increasingly used by lenders in lower-risk transactions, Polito is also sceptical whether their influence will ultimately threaten the human factor.

“Take those with a grain of salt, knowing that what a platform spits out may not be completely accurate in the same way that what a professional appraiser might conclude the property is worth,” he said.

“An appraiser uses all of their senses as part of the analysis. An appraiser sees what the analytical computer doesn’t see.”

items.title: National Bank acquires Embark in $226M education savings deal
items.description: The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella
items.content: <p>The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639299339464127761.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella
items.body:
National Bank of Canada has agreed to acquire Embark Student Corp. for approximately $226 million, gaining a digitally driven national education savings platform and more than $6 billion in assets under management.

The deal brings National Bank roughly 436,000 Registered Education Savings Plan (RESP) beneficiaries managed through Embark’s tech-enabled platform, with closing expected by mid-fiscal 2027, subject to court and regulatory approvals.

The transaction extends National Bank’s retail banking reach into Ontario and Western Canada — markets where the Montreal-headquartered lender has pursued a series of strategic acquisitions, including its 2024 agreement to acquire Canadian Western Bank.

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the deal signals a wider industry shift: the country’s major banks are competing not just on rates but on the depth of integrated family financial planning they can offer — from housing debt to education savings to retirement.

“We are happy to see Embark joining National Bank,” said Nancy Paquet, Executive Vice-President, Wealth Management at National Bank of Canada.

“This transaction is strongly aligned with our savings and investment advisory strategy for our clients, combining Embark’s digital capabilities with National Bank’s strengths to deliver a best-in-class education savings experience and expand our presence across Canada. We look forward to welcoming Embark’s employees and clients in the next months.”

Read more: RBC to acquire Australian fund manager Yarra Capital in 2027 deal

A platform built for record RESP adoption

The acquisition arrives as Canadian families turn to RESPs in growing numbers.

Statistics Canada’s 2025 Survey of Approaches to Educational Planning, released February 20, found that 89% of children with dedicated education savings held an RESP that year, up from 85% in 2020.

At the same time, financial anxiety now grips roughly 60% of Canadians, making education savings an increasingly contested priority in household budgets that brokers are helping clients navigate day to day.

“Joining forces with National Bank accelerates our mission to make education savings accessible to every Canadian parent,” said Andrew Lo, CEO and President of Embark Student Corp.

“This partnership reflects a shared commitment to that goal, and it’s why this is the right fit at the right time. We are excited to continue delivering best-in-class RESP services and advice, now alongside National Bank.”

Read more: Tru Cooperative Bank broadens its broker reach across Canada

Transaction structure and what clients can expect

The deal will be implemented by way of a plan of arrangement under the Canada Business Corporations Act and requires approval from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

National Bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is expected to decline by approximately 10 basis points on closing.

The acquisition price of approximately $226 million is subject to working capital adjustments.

Embark customers will see no immediate changes. Daily operations, government grant applications, and RESP investment management all continue as normal.

Founded in 1859 and headquartered in Montreal, Québec, National Bank of Canada is one of Canada’s six systemically important banks. It reported a 23% rise in third-quarter 2026 net income and held approximately $635 billion in assets as at July 31. 

The company employs roughly 37,000 people across its five business segments: Personal Banking, Commercial Banking, Wealth Management, Capital Markets, and ABA Bank. 

Embark Student Corp., meanwhile, is Canada’s digital education savings and planning company, headquartered in Toronto. It manages RESPs for approximately 436,000 beneficiaries nationwide and holds more than $6 billion in assets under management.

Registered as a Scholarship Plan Dealer across Canada, Embark provides end-to-end investment management, government grant administration, and digital savings tools to Canadian families.

It operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Embark Student Foundation, a not-for-profit Canadian corporation that serves as the current promoter of the Embark plans.

items.title: How Canada’s mortgage market has handled the renewal wave
items.description: Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown
items.content: <p>Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639299340826703449.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown
items.body:
At MortgageFest Canada, we caught up with Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, to hear what lenders are discussing with brokers – and why the mortgage market to date has been able to withstand the wave of renewals some feared could cause significant challenges for the market.

[00:00] We had a road map at the beginning of the year of tools that would take about two to three years to get done. We got them all done last month. How many brokers in here are doing TikToks and they're actually seeing a benefit from it? I think everyone got really worried about it so they got really good at preparing for it. The renewal cliff doesn't exist to the extreme. We're not going to just talk about mortgages. We're going to talk about everything.

[00:32] Fergal McAlinden: Now, so we are back with Grant Armstrong, Chief Growth Officer at Wealth One Bank of Canada. As we were saying, Grant, really busy start to the year for everybody. It's been a, well, not start to the year, it's been an interesting year for everyone. Talk about your message to brokers today. There are plenty of them here. What are you guys talking about?

[00:51] Grant Armstrong: Yeah, the biggest thing we're trying to do is explain to brokers who we are. Wealth One Bank is actually Canada's fastest growing bank. So what we want to be able to do is understand what our message is, what we're focusing on, our goals, how we can help the industry, how we can partner with brokers better, but also just why we're different.

[01:08] I mean, it's incredible. The number of organizations that are here today. I do remember the very first event about four years ago and it would fit maybe two rows. You've sold out an incredible location here. So, we want to tell people why we're different, why we believe in them, what we're trying to help them with, and go forward from there.

[01:26] Fergal McAlinden: It always strikes me that for events like this, one of the biggest advantages for both brokers and lenders is that you get a chance to talk to each other about maybe some of the pain points, things that are going well, things that are going badly. Is there anything that you commonly see with brokers or agents that you think you'd like to get the message out that needs to be different or that maybe they're not doing that they should be doing at the moment?

[01:45] Grant Armstrong: Yeah, I think this is a great opportunity to sit down with brokers and talk to them about what they're doing, but we're doing it a little differently. We're trying to understand what their pain points are. And the biggest pain points that we're hearing from brokers is the ever-changing policies, the ever-changing rules, the ever-changing processes that lenders are introducing.

[02:03] Every lender in the room is just trying to be more efficient, more productive. So every single week a lender has changed how you submit a deal, what forms you need, what documents. Brokers are struggling to keep up with that information. So what we're trying to do is actually, we did all of our changes earlier this year and we're actually trying to tell everyone we're status quo.

[02:23] All the changes that we're doing are back-end changes, but they get to see the benefit. So we brought in AI, for example. We're using AI to build tools. We had a road map at the beginning of the year of tools that would take about two to three years to get done, and we got them all done last month.

[02:38] So that's what we're doing on the back end. We want to hear what their pain points are, make sure they know that we're changing what we do in the back, but it's not impacting them except for all the positive sides of that.

[02:48] The other part is we're trying to get people to understand the credit environment. Between regulators, between people south of the border, between wars, it all impacts mortgage interest rates, it all impacts process, it all impacts risk. So how, as a lender, as a Schedule I bank, are we interpreting that and how are we putting it back out there? Those are the conversations we're having.

[03:12] Fergal McAlinden: It's interesting you mention that. You and I have been talking over the years, probably starting around COVID time. We had record low interest rates, we had economic turmoil, all that. Then we moved into rate spikes. There was talk about the renewal cliff and all that kind of thing. Then we have all the geopolitical tensions that we've seen over the past couple of years, condo challenges and more.

[03:32] What about the market for 2026? How are you viewing it? And anything you're keeping in mind navigating the current outlook?

[03:38] Grant Armstrong: I'm going to sound like a broken record. I've been saying this for four years. The markets are good. And what I love about what brokers have done is they've diversified.

[03:47] A lot of people say, "Oh, the market's slow." No. Purchase transactions are slow in some areas, but refinancing, switching, consolidating, improvements, investor opportunities, there are brokers I was talking to the other day that have paired up with wealth management organizations to be able to help people fund investments and fund savings.

[04:04] So the diversity of what brokers are doing has kind of negated the market trends. Ten or fifteen years ago you could see seasonality. That's gone. It's now an opportunity that sits 60, 90, 120 days in front of you. So lenders that can actually adapt to that change and keep their processes, policies, and marketing top of mind are benefiting from that.

[04:28] The other conversation I had a long chat about yesterday was brokers getting much more into marketing. It used to be business groups, handshakes, and realtors. But social media. I mean, how many brokers in here are doing TikToks and they're actually seeing a benefit from it?

[04:43] So, I think 2026 is going to end on a high. Not to dampen the market, I think rates will probably go up in October. I think the governor basically alluded to that without alluding to it the other day. We'll see shifts.

[04:56] But what you can also see on the fixed-rate side of the market is they've already been going up. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last 60 to 90 days. Bond rates are up 60 points. Everything's been going up already. It's just a natural part of the market.

[05:12] Fergal McAlinden: What about when it comes to the renewal? We've talked about that so much over the past few years. We were all looking to the cliff that we talked about in 2025 and 2026. Do you get the impression that it's been more manageable than we maybe thought a couple of years back, or what's your look on that one?

[05:26] Grant Armstrong: I think it was a war cry. I think what it was is, we're going to anchor around this. The reality is 20% to 40% of mortgages renew every two years. That's just the reality. Shorter terms have driven that number up.

[05:40] I think everyone got really worried about it, so they got really good at preparing for it. And I think that preparation has taken the noise out of it. The big renewal cliff was in 2021 when rates were around 1.99% to 2.49% and then in a year or two they were renewing at 6% to 7%.

[05:58] That was the renewal cliff. That happened to alternative lenders, private lenders, and others. But prime lenders took three- and five-year terms. They skipped it. So they were able to start renewing again as rates started to come down.

[06:10] We're in normal rates today. We're not in obscenely high rates. We're in normal rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn't exist to the extreme, but it's something we need to be aware of.

[06:21] And the stress test, as much as many people don't love it, worked. Every customer was qualified at at least 5.25%. Rates are below 5.25%, so they should be able to handle it.

[06:32] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah. The stress test, I feel, is always the one regulatory thing that a lot of brokers pointed to and said this should go or it served its purpose. But its purpose was to do what it did, I guess, and it really helped.

[06:45] Grant Armstrong: It's a barrier, don't get me wrong. The stress test does limit some deals, but it's necessary. It constrained people from going out too far. Some of those customers that didn't have a stress test, when rates were 1.99%, would be getting three- and four-million-dollar mortgages. They'd be in a lot of trouble now. So it's a necessary tool that was required.

[07:05] Fergal McAlinden: Sure. Okay, so Wealth One. Anything that you're really excited to share today? Anything coming down the line that we should be keeping an eye on?

[07:12] Grant Armstrong: Wealth One is advancing beyond just being a mortgage lender. Last week we actually did a massive campaign in Toronto. We're helping Canadians save. We have Canada's highest-rate non-promotional savings account. We're helping Canadians on both sides of that balance sheet.

[07:28] I don't want to give too much away, but we've got a few more enhancements on those products. We also want to see how we can help brokers be much more involved in that. I think brokers have this incredible opportunity to sit in front of customers.

[07:41] It started with mortgages. Creditor insurance came out a couple of years after that, and it hasn't really crossed into other product lines. I want to see how we can actually position brokers as that adviser to the customer and give them more tools, more products in front of them.

[07:55] So we have a number of changes that are going to amplify our business on both sides of the balance sheet, but we want to be able to have that conversation with brokers about both sides. That's the big change you're going to see with us. We're not going to just talk about mortgages. We're going to talk about everything and really make sure that brokers are advised on everything they need to give customers.

[08:10] Fergal McAlinden: Okay, perfect. Last question, Grant, before I let you go. You've been at a few of these events. You were here when it was the Mortgage Summit. Now we're at Mortgage Fest. What's your impression of the event so far?

[08:19] Grant Armstrong: Oh, it's incredible. I was talking to somebody. Four years ago, when you planned it, there were maybe 230 people that might make it, and it was almost a thousand. This is a must-see event.

[08:33] If you're a broker and you want to talk to lenders, you want to talk to other people, you want to hear great speakers, you want to get insights, this is the place you need to be. And as a lender, I wouldn't be anywhere else.

[08:45] I congratulate you guys and the team. You had a mission four years ago. You gave me an opportunity to be part of that four years ago. I was on stage at your first one. I'm happy to look forward to the next 10 or 20 that you do and be there and support each one of them.

[09:01] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Well, we're looking forward to seeing what's next from you guys from Wealth One and seeing what's in store for the rest of the year. So, thank you very much.

[09:08] Grant Armstrong: Thanks, guys.

items.body:
VANCOUVER — The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of "mounting headwinds" for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.

The association says in its fourth-quarter forecast that sales are expected to fall 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 levels, to just over 67,000 units sold.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson says in a statement that prospective buyers this year had several reasons to hesitate, including an oil-price shock, trade tensions with the United States, slower immigration and rising interest rates.

The forecast says active listings in B.C. are at their highest levels since 2015, and new-home inventory is also elevated.

It predicts that the supply pressure will push the average home price down 1.2 per cent to just over $941,000.

The forecast calls for a "modest recovery" in 2027 with sales projected to increase 7.2 per cent, but Ogmundson says that's in anticipation of a decline in the impacts of new U.S. tariffs and reductions in fixed mortgage rates.

"Hopefully, a calming of these headwinds next year should stimulate housing activity, which, paired with flattening inventories, is expected to drive price growth of 2.4 per cent in 2027, bringing the provincial average price to $964,200," the forecast says, adding it is anticipating a "long-awaited rebound" in the Lower Mainland market.

Greater Vancouver home sales are projected to reach 23,000 units this year, down 3 per cent from the year before, while the Fraser Valley is forecast to see a 4.4 per cent decrease to 11,000 units.

The largest decline is expected in the Chilliwack area of the Lower Mainland, with unit sales falling from 2,300 last year to 1,900 this year, an 18-per-cent decrease.

"Following a 2025 that saw the weakest year of sales in over a decade, faint signs of a 2026 recovery were thwarted by a resurgent oil price shock and further escalation in Canada’s trade war with the United States," the forecast says.

"With population growth expected to remain subdued through 2027, B.C. faces limited capacity to grow at trend levels."

items.title: Eight Properties Owned By Valour Group’s District REIT Placed Under Receivership
items.description:
A portfolio of rental buildings in Ontario and New Brunswick owned by privately-managed District REIT have been placed under receivership, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

District REIT was founded by Richard Hall and Carmen Campagnaro, who also founded Burlington-based developer Valour Group, which itself had a 1,500-unit project in Ajax placed under receivership earlier this year, as previously reported by STOREYS.

“As a Canadian trust, District REIT strategically acquires income-producing properties across key markets in Canada, with a foundation in Southwestern Ontario,” said District REIT on its corporate website.

“Our expansion into New Brunswick reflects our long-term vision of geographic diversification as we identify high-potential opportunities from coast to coast,” they added. “We strategically select assets that align with our growth objectives and deliver value to Unitholders — from thriving urban centres like Toronto to emerging communities like Ayr and Saint John, and beyond.”

Their corporate website lists 29 properties in their portfolio, which are predominantly multi-family properties — apartment buildings and townhouse communities — and industrial properties.

The properties that are subject to the receivership proceedings are:

1. 3967 Savoy Street, London, Ontario: 47 units

2. 15 Gamble Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 27 units

3. 33 Gamble Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 28 units

4. 40 Beaty Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 27 units

5. 11 West Street, Brantford, Ontario: 26 units

6. 225 Riddell Street, Woodstock, Ontario: 56 units

7. 33 and 45 Jack Street, St. John, New Brunswick: 48 units

8. 133-135 Woodhaven Drive, St. John, New Brunswick: 48 units

The eight properties total to 307 units, 209 of which are leased, for a total occupancy rate of 68%. The properties are together bringing in $306,271.51 in gross rent.

The first seven properties are beneficially owned by District REIT Limited Partnership, while the eighth is beneficially owned by East Park Limited Partnership, all through individual holding companies.

The Insolvency

The receivership proceeding was initiated by CMLS Financial, a non-bank lender that was founded in Vancouver in 1974 and acquired by Montreal-based digital mortgage lender Nesto in 2024.

CMLS Financial provided a first-ranking mortgage for each of the eight properties between February 2022 and December 2024, each for a principal amount between $5,000,000 and $18,000,000.

According to the lender, there have been numerous defaults across the various loan agreements, with District REIT ceasing to make required monthly payments pertaining to all the properties beginning around April 2026. In some of the cases, CMLS says the owners also defaulted by failing to provide an energy efficiency attestation and failing to pay property taxes.

CMLS says it issued a formal demand for payment on June 2, after which the owners proposed a “stabilization plan.” That plan included selling some of the properties while retaining others. The owners also told CMLS that the properties were facing a $4.4 million operating shortfall and were not expected to be cash flow positive until February 2027.

“The Stablization Plan was (and remains) unacceptable to CMLS,” said the lender in an receivership application dated October 2. “Following CMLS’ rejection of the Stabilization Plan, the Debtors through their counsel submitted further without prejudice proposals that were also unacceptable to CMLS. CMLS in turn provided forbearance terms that were not accepted by the Debtors.”

CMLS Financial was owed over $78.8 million as of October 5, with interest continuing to accrue, and the Ontario Superior Court granted the receivership on October 28.

District REIT

Although they were ultimately unsuccessful, District REIT filed a response in court opposing CLMS Financial’s receivership application, with Co-Founder Richard Hall revealing many details about the REIT in an affidavit dated October 13.

According to Hall, the eight properties are beneficially owned by District REIT Limited Partnership, which is in turn 99.9% owned by retail investors.

“The overwhelming majority of the equity in the District REIT is held by local retail investors who invested in support of the Valour Group’s mission to create housing in Ontario’s secondary markets,” said Hall.

Hall said that District REIT currently has approximately 850 unique investors and that it’s portfolio of 28 properties have a total appraised value of $218.36 million as of December 31, 2025.

“The investors in the District REIT contributed approximately $86 million in invested capital,” said Hall. “As a result of the market conditions described below, I estimate that the equity value attributable to those investors today is approximately $50 million on an appraisal basis, and in the range of approximately $25 million to $30 million on the basis of the sale prices currently being achieved in the market.”

Explaining their liquidity constraints, Hall pointed to market conditions, interest rates, and tariffs, among other things. Hall also said they were in the process of selling various properties and was anticipating sale prices that would more than cover CMLS’s expected shortfalls.

“The only real exposure CMLS faces is the projected shortfall on the three Toronto Properties,” said Hall. “A receivership does nothing to cure that shortfall — it increases it, by adding receivership costs and a forced-sale discount to the same properties.”

Those additional costs, Hall said, “would fall first on the District REIT’s investors” and “A 20% discount on receivership sales, together with the costs of the receivership, would in my estimation eliminate that equity entirely.” Furthermore, he added that placing the eight properties under receivership would “put the viability of the District REIT as a whole at serious risk.”

The Owners

According to CMLS, the owners are facing “significant cash flow issues” and the troubles “appear to be part of greater organization-wide issues facing Richard and Carmen’s various businesses,” including two other properties — 27 Bold Street in Hamilton and 2158 Lilnan Court in Burlington — being placed under receivership.

27 Bold Street is a 32-unit rental building called The Oscar On Bold that was developed by Valour Group, which beneficially owns the property through Oscar Bold Inc. The building became the subject of a CBC News story in June 2025 after tenants went weeks without gas and air conditioning. The lender that initiated the receivership in October 2025 was Tandia Financial Credit Union and the property was listed for sale earlier this year by Colliers.

2158 Lilnan Court is a 7-unit rental building that was originally constructed in 1958 and beneficially owned by Valour Group through Lilnan Ltd. The lender that initiated the receivership, also in October 2025, was Royal Bank of Canada, and the property is currently listed for sale by JLL.

According to CMLS Financial, District REIT has “laid off a significant portion of its workforce in an attempt to manage its cash constraints” and Richard Hall and Carmen Campagnaro are also subject to bankruptcy applications commenced against them in their personal capacities.

In the aforementioned court response, Hall did not deny the existence of these other proceedings, but said they have no impact on CMLS Financial and that he and Campagnaro intend to oppose the bankruptcy applications. As for the layoffs at the REIT, Hall acknowledged the workforce reduction, but said that the reduction has not impaired its management of the properties.

Nonetheless, the eight properties are now under receivership and the court-appointed Receiver has published an FAQ for unitholders in District REIT.

items.title: Applications Open For New Program Levelling Up Canada’s Project Leaders
items.description:
Canada’s push to build is well underway, and the major projects now being planned and delivered need people truly prepared to lead them.

For many organizations, those people are already on the team, bringing with them 10 to 15 years of experience, a strong track record running projects, and the ambition to take the next step.

Now, a new program is poised to prepare those leaders. The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy, launched by the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, is the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. Applications are now open, and are being reviewed on a rolling basis.

The academy offers what neither an MBA nor a project management certification does: a specialized focus on major-project leadership, from building teams across the many organizations that share a major project to negotiating the conflict that so often arises. Developed in collaboration with industry and government leaders, the program brings public and private sector participants together, so each cohort leaves with a national network of senior peers.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship and a capstone project. Participants work through a real issue from their own professional contexts with mentor support, so the value builds as the program progresses. Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

For leaders outside Ontario, the in-person portion comes down to three three-day modules, with the rest of the program delivered online. The academy is designed to grow into a national program, delivered locally across the country. The first cohort, launching April 13, 2027, will bring together an intentionally diverse group of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects, so a participant from Calgary or Vancouver leaves with connections well beyond their own market.

“A lot is being staked right now on being able to build big things,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Academic Co-Director at the Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy. The projects themselves have grown more complex, too. In Siemiatycki’s words, today’s major project is “an IT project wrapped in steel,” involving ever more parties, and ever more technology.

That pressure is especially visible out West. Insights from Altus Group’s 2026 Canadian Cost Guide found overall construction costs in Calgary and Edmonton rose 4% or more year over year, even as they fell in Toronto and Vancouver. Further, BuildForce Canada projects that 43,700 of Alberta’s construction workers — or, about 21% of the province’s 2025 construction labour force — will retire by 2035, just as non-residential construction is expected to grow. All the while, the Canadian Construction Association’s summer 2026 economic report points to growing use of sector-specific tariffs and local procurement measures, along with the domestic requirements that come with them.

These aren’t easy conditions, but they’re exactly the conditions the curriculum is built for. Alongside leadership and negotiation, participants work on commercial leadership, procurement, and governance, as well as the behavioural biases that lead projects to underestimate costs, all skills that matter more when budgets are under pressure and experienced people are leaving the industry.

For the companies delivering those projects, much of that complexity turns into risk. The way today’s contracts are written, Siemiatycki says, companies take on a huge amount of it — especially in construction — and when a project goes badly, they absorb the cost. That makes training the people in charge a strategic business decision. Giving leaders the most modern techniques to guide projects of this nature, he says, “is a risk mitigation strategy.” With tuition priced in line with comparable academies in the UK and Australia, it’s an investment in the people carrying that risk.

For organizations deciding who will lead their next major project, the inaugural cohort is a chance to prepare that person now. Leaders can apply directly, and organizations can nominate a member of their team to apply.

Spots are limited. Apply by November 30th to secure a 20% discount.

items.description:

The post Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s Budget 2026 adds 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, but the housing demand boost is limited as recipients already live here.
items.body:
Canada is adjusting its immigration plan after a recent slowdown in population growth. Budget 2026 shows the country is adding 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027. On top of regular admissions and existing programs, the total can exceed 580,000 spots by the end of next year. However, this won’t add much to housing demand, as the extra spaces aim to retain people already here and reduce population churn.

Canadian Immigration Targets Vs Reality

Before diving into the changes, let’s clarify that immigration targets aren’t hard numbers. Ottawa isn’t just making a DoorDash order for 10,000 Guinean students; it sets a target. Meeting that target depends on global demand, domestic processing, and applicant follow-through.

IRCC data shows only 216,600 regular permanent resident admissions in the first 8 months of 2026. That’s just 57% of the target with only a third of the year left, making that a tough goal to hit. Canadian taxpayers actually spent millions to create that post-pandemic study permit surge. Ottawa’s caps only appeared after applications cratered, as qualified demand was exhausted. But don’t let that ruin the narrative of unlimited growth that policymakers want you to believe.

It’s important to understand that immigration targets are similar to a public company’s earnings projections, but instead of boosting a stock price, they bolster Canada’s projected economic growth and access to debt. Whether global demand is there to fulfil the targets remains to be seen. Now let’s move on to the changes.

Canada Trims Temporary Arrivals, Adds 200k Permanent Resident Spots

Budget 2026 reveals fewer new temporary arrivals and more permanent spots. The 2027 immigration targets maintain 380,000 regular permanent admissions and 370,000 new temporary arrivals annually through 2029. That’s a 3.9% reduction (15,000 spots) in new temporary arrivals from the 2026 target, as previously announced. The big change is additional targeted permanent resident spots.

Canada plans to add up to 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, up to 100,000 for workers and their families, and up to 100,000 for specified humanitarian and family applicants. Combined with the existing target, it lifts potential permanent resident admissions to 580,000, 52.6% higher than the regular admission target. That’s on top of the earlier initiatives that targeted the transition of 148,000 temporary to permanent residents in 2026-27. Admissions could exceed 580,000 with those earlier initiatives.

Interestingly, it’s accompanied by a reduction to the Federal High Skilled admissions program, which will fall from the previously planned target of 111,000 people to 100,000. However, provincial nominee admissions will rise by 2,500 to 95,000, while the Atlantic Immigration Program rises from 4,000 to 6,000 targeted admissions. Rather than an outright reduction, it looks like Ottawa is hoping to better target regional growth.

More Permanent Residents Don’t Mean More Population Growth

The addition of 200,000 permanent residents won’t directly add to aggregate demand, especially housing. These admissions will only shift people from temporary residents to permanent ones, so their consumption is already reflected today. This distinction was also made clear by the PBO earlier this year, when they reported 48% of permanent residents in 2025 were previously international students or temporary workers.

As we explained earlier this year, Ottawa promised to reduce non-permanent residents as a share of the population, but was initially light on the details. Part of that plan is to turn temporary residents into permanent ones, which the PBO found necessary under the previous plan to hit the target of below 5% by the end of 2027, a delay of a year. Budget 2026 appears to be buying policymakers some more room to help them hit that target.

items.title: Insider: Budget 2026 Opens Up Financing For Small Rental Builders
items.description:
A developer who shelved a small rental project over financing has a reason to price it again.

Budget 2026 gives newly built triplexes and fourplexes access to insured loans of up to 90% of completed value. It also lets private insurers cover buildings with five to 50 units.

Budget 2026, tabled November 5, pairs those changes with more money for Build Canada Homes. For a smaller builder, the mortgage rules are the part to take to a lender first: how much cash would the project need up front, and could the finished building support the loan?

Keep the rent assumptions where they were for that comparison. Otherwise, it becomes hard to tell whether the financing has improved the project or the spreadsheet has simply become more optimistic.

Different rules on either side of five units

The Department of Finance's technical rules take effect for insurance applications lenders submit on or after February 1, 2027. The unit count determines which rules apply.

For buildings with five to 50 units, term financing requires a minimum debt coverage ratio of 1.15 for a five-year term or 1.10 for a ten-year term. Borrowers need net worth equal to at least 25% of the requested loan, with a $100,000 minimum, based on Canadian assets. Separately titled properties cannot be bundled to meet the unit requirement.

Construction loans are assessed separately. Insurers set their own debt-servicing criteria during construction; the prescribed amortization and debt coverage requirements apply to term financing. Borrowers using the new three- and four-unit option also have to pass personal qualification tests for the long-term mortgage.

A fourplex and a six-unit building can face quite different borrowing limits on the same site. The six-unit design may qualify for a longer amortization, but it may also cost more to build. Compare the extra debt with the extra cost and rent before choosing the larger project.

Compare the new loans with CMHC

CMHC Standard Rental Housing already covers eligible properties with at least five units. It allows borrowing of up to 85% of value, with amortizations of up to 50 years for new construction and 40 years for existing properties.

MLI Select offers different terms in exchange for commitments to affordability, energy efficiency or accessibility. Eligible new construction can qualify for up to 95% loan-to-cost, depending on the points earned and the program's other requirements.

The new private-insurer rules add another option to that comparison. Be careful with the percentages: 90% of appraised value and 95% of project cost can produce quite different loan amounts.

Ask for offers that cover the same project and construction schedule. Compare the interest rate and insurance premium, then work through guarantees, reserve requirements and conditions on each draw. A larger approved loan can be less useful if its costs are higher or the money arrives too late to pay the contractor.

The rent limits the loan

Take a hypothetical new rental building worth $5 million, with annual net operating income of $225,000. At a 5% mortgage rate, a 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage, the income supports about $3.62 million of debt. A loan at 90% of the building's value would be $4.5 million.

That leaves a gap of roughly $881,000 between the advertised maximum and what the income can support.

Illustrative calculation: a $4.5-million value ceiling versus income-based capacity of about $4.25 million at 4%, $3.62 million at 5% and $3.13 million at 6%. Assumes 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage.

These calculations apply to the mortgage after construction. They use monthly payments and Canadian nominal rates compounded semi-annually, and exclude insurance premiums, fees and reserves. The rates are examples rather than lender quotes. An insurer may also use different income and expense assumptions when it assesses the property.

A builder can tie up less equity and still be taking on more risk. The loan has to be serviced through vacancies, repairs and a slower-than-expected lease-up. Those expenses belong in the operating budget before anyone calculates how much debt the building can carry.

Get the construction loan and the permanent mortgage assessed together. If the finished property cannot support enough mortgage debt to repay the construction lender, the builder has to find the difference.

Build Canada Homes funding starts later

The budget proposes another $13 billion in cash capital for Build Canada Homes over ten years, beginning in 2028–29. That would bring its capitalization to $45 billion. Ottawa's target is 200,000 homes over the next decade; delivery will depend on projects moving through approvals and construction.

It also proposes $1.5 billion over four years from 2027–28 for infrastructure on federal land, plus $387.4 million in later years. A builder considering a partnership needs to know when a particular site will be serviced and when the money will be available. Procurement terms will determine who can take part.

Source: Department of Finance missing-middle backgrounder and Budget 2026 Chapter 3, November 5, 2026. Fiscal-year funding starts are not home-completion dates.

Public land and long-term capital can help build housing for people whose rents cannot cover the cost of new construction. The operating budget needs funding, too. Taxes, maintenance and repairs continue long after the building opens.

For market rental projects, the effect will depend partly on the supply of buildable sites. Easier financing can help developers start viable projects. Where land and approvals are scarce, buyers may instead use the extra borrowing room to bid more for the same sites.

Reprice the project before bidding more for land

Run the available financing options against the same operating budget. Then confirm which lenders and insurers will offer them, what they need to approve an application and how the construction loan converts to a term mortgage. February 1 is the start date for lender submissions, so allow time for approval and funding.

For a small developer, the useful result is a loan commitment that makes a viable project possible.

If the numbers work only after raising the projected rents or cutting the repair allowance, the financing problem is still there.

Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada To Lift Ban On Foreign Buyers of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s Budget 2026 will extend the foreign buyer home ban but exempt new homes. Billions in taxpayer back incentives were used to create supply with the narrative of bringing prices lower. Now that developers are sitting on near record inventory that’s still out of reach for local incomes, the plan has changed. Policymakers argue demand from non-residents will boost affordability by helping to create new supply. The problem? The ban was extended because non-resident speculators were flooding into new homes in the first place.

Canadian Unemployment Climbs, Nearly 1 in 3 Struggle To Buy Necessities

Headline employment data looked largely unchanged but the devil was in the details. Statistics Canada (StatCan) reported jobs were relatively unchanged in October. Unemployment still climbed 0.2 points to 6.7% though, as more people sought work. The worst news was in a special supplement that revealed almost 1 in 3 struggle to pay for necessities, rolling back improvements made since 2022. The headline may show little change in jobs, but the details show more unemployment for longer terms, and less financial security.

The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble

Investors in both Canada and the US are planning a lot of data centers. The rising and revolutionary use of AI means more will be needed, but just how many? Crunching the numbers reveals that just 1 in 5 data centers announced have actual progress. Investors and the politicians they’ve elected are blaming an energy shortage, but we found most haven’t applied for a utilities hookup. We take a deep dive into the multi-trillion speculative data center real estate bubble and the tax changes that have them vying to become landlords of the internet.

Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share

Banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from Canada’s real estate bubble popping. The bank’s median allowance for mortgage losses has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, tripling since Q2 2019. The top 25% of banks preparing for losses has set aside nearly double the median, and the most since 2015. While economists at many banks are saying the bottom is near, their risk departments are preparing for it to worsen in the near-term.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Dropped Over $360k Since Peak

The price of a typical home in Greater Toronto slipped 0.1% to $915,400 in October. Losses extended further as weak sales and lofty inventory combined to create further downward pressure. This likely surprises many, as prices have already trimmed 28.4% (-$363k) from the 2022 peak. However, the supply balance suggests things may get worse before they improve.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Real Estate Prices Slip, Just 3% Higher Than 2017 Peak

The price of a home across Greater Vancouver fell 0.7% to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% lower than last year. Weak sales and lofty inventory has pushed the region out of stagnation and into a second-leg of a correction. How low can prices go? It’s not clear, but it’s worth noting that at this level, the price of a typical home is only 3% higher than it was at the 2017 peak. Nearly a decade of stagnation and the market’s indicators are slanted towards further declines.

items.body:
Canada has one weird trick to help with housing affordability—sell the new homes you can’t afford to foreign buyers. That’s not a mistake; it’s the pitch in Canada’s Budget 2026, which will extend the foreign buyer ban until 2029. However, this time they plan to exempt foreign buyers to clear the stagnating inventory. Ottawa frames this as a win for affordability despite all evidence suggesting otherwise.

Canada To Allow Foreign Buying of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s existing ban on foreign ownership is set to expire in just under two months. Despite quietly inserting exemptions in the ban just 86 days after the law took effect, policymakers say they’ll renew the policy. Sort of.

“[Canada will] extend the ban on foreign purchases of existing residential properties for two years, to January 1, 2029, while exempting new residential properties,” reads Budget 2026.

That’s right. Policymakers plan to reopen foreign buying of new homes, the segment that sparked the ban in the first place. The doublespeak doesn’t end there.

“This would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply,” explains Budget 2026.

Ottawa Wants Foreign Investment To Help Build More Housing

More supply was supposed to bring down prices, but that didn’t happen. Billions in tax incentives stimulated building new supply, but prices remain out of reach. New home sales in cities like Toronto are near record lows, while developers sit on record inventory. Weak demand hasn’t brought prices down much—in fact, home prices are near highs in most provinces. With home prices requiring nearly double the median household income to buy at these levels, Canadians can’t afford to buy a home.

Despite years of warnings that weak sales will slow construction, new building remains elevated. In fact, elsewhere in Budget 2026, policymakers boasted about their contribution to roughly 250,000 annualized new home starts in the first half of 2026, 20% above the 2015-2019 average. However, the narrative of slow sales threatening new home construction has seen taxpayers back billions in developer bailouts. Now Ottawa is hoping foreign buyers will be a further bailout for developers.

Foreign Buyers Were Concentrated In New Homes Before The Ban

Policymakers may be claiming that ignorance is strength, and the foreign buyer ban was always to target existing stock. But a quick trip down the data memory lane makes it clear pretty fast that new homes were the primary issue.

The 2020 property records that led Ottawa to create the ban show a concentration in new condos (post-2016 builds). Almost 1 in 7 (13.4%) of BC’s new condos were owned by non-residents that year, the highest among the four provinces studied. Non-residents also piled into Nova Scotia (11.1%), New Brunswick (10%), and Ontario (9.2%). Most of these new condos were in major cities.

Toronto may sound light with non-residents owning 7.7% of new condos, according to 2019 property records. However, keep in mind the region represented 1 in 6 home sales across Canada then. Even so, it looks tiny in contrast to the 13.6% in Vancouver. Of course, Canada’s current housing minister MP Gregor Robertson doesn’t need a refresher—the Vancouver-based minister was the Mayor of Vancouver at the peak of its foreign buying boom.

Despite arguing in favour of foreign capital in housing recently, he sang a different tune back then. Back in 2016, he blasted the Province for not imposing taxes to slow buying. “Middle-class Canadians being able to buy a house in Vancouver and Toronto, those days have probably passed because the [foreign buyer] interventions didn’t come,” said then-Mayor Robertson.

Well, if middle-class families can’t afford housing in the rest of Canada now, why not go all in?

Canada Wants Its Foreign Buyers Back, But Will They Return?

First off, when Canada says “non-resident investment,” it almost entirely means Chinese investors, representing roughly 70% of that demand. These buyers were driven by a reputation of a financial system free from political persecution, wealthy students looking for prestigious education, and a scramble of capital looking to be laundered in Canadian housing—much of it fleeing China’s anti-corruption crackdown.

Vancouver’s foreign home buyer boom began when wealthy Hong Kongers sought investment safety. Canada’s financial system is no longer viewed as a system free from political persecution. The shift extends beyond Canada, with Beijing advising China’s elites to pull their investments out of Western countries. The country recently tightened outbound investment even further.

China used to be Canada’s number one source of international students. Canada has since traded in its prestigious reputation for one better known as a back door to immigration. China has since gone from being the number one source of foreign students to falling behind Guinea. Maybe Guinean students will fuel the new housing demand.

The opaque system that made Canadian real estate the perfect asset for money laundering has also since come under scrutiny. The use of Canada’s banks to launder money through real estate was well known, facilitating billions in transfers. Canadian banks have since received a few slaps on the wrist, paid billions in fines, and come under much tighter oversight. Darn it. Why are regulators so anti-supply, preventing affordability!

None of this is to say that Canada won’t see a rise in the number of foreign buyers. However, it’s unlikely to be from the source that drove investor demand before. A new market may be developing, especially since it’s common to sell new homes cheaper overseas to prevent local prices from falling. That might even be more enticing if Vancouver’s Condo King negotiated the foreign buyer tax incentives he was working on with the PM.

items.title: Canadian Unemployment Climbs, Nearly 1 in 3 Struggle To Buy Necessities
items.description:
